articles.summary: Asim Munir | Biography, Army Chief, Pakistan, India, Afghanistan, Balochistan, & Kashmir  Britannica
articles.full_text:
(born 1968?, Rawalpindi?, Pakistan) is a Pakistani military officer who has served as the chief of Army Staff of Pakistan since November 2022. An intelligence veteran, he has also served as the director general of Military Intelligence (MI) and the director general of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), the country’s top intelligence agency. In May 2025 he was promoted to the rank of Field Marshal, the highest military rank in the country, while continuing to serve as the chief of Army Staff. He is the second person in Pakistan’s history to hold this rank after Mohammad Ayub Khan in 1959. In November 2025 the Parliament of Pakistan passed the 27th constitutional amendment, which elevated Munir to the newly created post of chief of defense forces, allowing him to oversee all branches of the armed forces such as the Air Force and Navy. The amendment also allows him to retain the privileges associated with his rank as Field Marshal indefinitely, effectively granting him lifelong immunity from criminal prosecution.
Early life and military career
Although Munir’s date and place of birth are unclear, media reports indicate he was born in 1968 in Rawalpindi, the location of the army’s headquarters and the capital of Pakistan from 1959 to 1969. His father was a schoolteacher and an imam (Muslim cleric). In 1986 Munir graduated from the Officers Training School at Mangla, Pakistan, where he was awarded the Sword of Honour for being the top cadet of his cohort. He was subsequently commissioned into the Pakistan Army and was posted to the Frontier Force Regiment, an infantry unit. He holds a master’s degree from the National Defence University in Islamabad, and he completed courses from military institutions in Japan and Malaysia. At one point in his career Munir served as a military attaché in Saudi Arabia. During this time he reportedly learned the Qurʾān and became a ḥāfiẓ—a title given to those who can recite every passage in the Qurʾān from memory, signifying immense spiritual achievement.
After several years of service and holding various leadership positions in the army, Munir became director general of MI in 2017. In October 2018 he was appointed director general of the ISI but was removed after about eight months, reportedly on Prime Minister Imran Khan’s insistence. The reason for his removal was not made public, although media reports speculated about tensions between the two.
In February 2019, while Munir was serving as ISI chief, tensions between India and Pakistan deteriorated after a suicide bomber rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into an Indian Central Reserve Police Force convoy in Pulwama, Jammu and Kashmir, killing some 40 security personnel. India’s government claimed that Pakistan was responsible for overseeing the attack, alleging that the Pakistan-based group Jaish-e-Mohammed—which claimed responsibility—received support from the ISI. Pakistan denied any role in the attack. The Indian military retaliated with air strikes on what it said was a Jaish-e-Mohammed training camp in Balakot, Pakistan.
Chief of Army Staff
In November 2022 Pakistani Pres. Arif Alvi appointed Munir as the country’s chief of Army Staff, the most influential position in both security and politics in Pakistan. The appointment came amid escalating tensions with former prime minister Khan, who had been ousted via a no-confidence motion in April and was shot in the leg in an apparent assassination attempt just weeks before Munir took office. In May 2023 Khan was arrested amid a flurry of legal cases, including corruption charges, shortly after accusing a top military officer of orchestrating the November attack, an accusation that the military publicly dismissed as “highly irresponsible and baseless.”
As army chief, Munir has taken a firm, often nationalist, stance on pressing security issues. He has emphasized a security-first approach, seeking to establish Pakistan as a regional military power. Focused on countering internal and external security threats, his approach combines assertive defense diplomacy—particularly toward India and Afghanistan—with strategic neutrality and economic self-reliance.
Munir has consistently blamed the Taliban government in Afghanistan for allowing Tehreek-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP; a group banned in Pakistan and designated as a terrorist organization by countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States) militants to launch attacks against Pakistan from Afghan territory. Tensions between the two neighbors surged in March 2024 after several militant groups, including the TTP, launched a series of terrorist attacks on China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) infrastructure, killing several Chinese nationals. In December the TTP claimed responsibility for an attack on a Pakistani military outpost in northwestern Pakistan near the country’s border with Afghanistan. The Pakistan military retaliated with air strikes against militant groups in Afghanistan. In January 2025 Munir asserted that the presence of TTP in Afghanistan was a major irritant in the two countries’ ties and called on the Taliban to end “the spread of terrorism in Pakistan from across the border.” Tensions came to a head in October when Pakistan carried out an air strike in Kabul that it said targeted the leader of the TTP, leading to skirmishes between the two countries (see Afghanistan-Pakistan Conflict [2025]). The Taliban denied the accusations of allowing safe haven for the TTP.
Munir has condemned the insurgency in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, where militants have pursued a separatist agenda for decades. In January 2024 Iran launched cross-border strikes against what it said were militant camps in Balochistan. Munir condemned the attacks and vowed to retaliate. A few days later Pakistan launched missile strikes on targets in Iran’s Sīstān va Balūchestān province. The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA)—which is designated as a terrorist organization by countries such as Pakistan, the United States, and the United Kingdom—was involved in attacks targeting CPEC infrastructure in 2024. Following a deadly train hijacking in March 2025 that left more than 20 passengers dead, for which the BLA claimed responsibility, Munir vowed to defeat separatist networks and facilitators operating in the region. Despite Balochistan’s location on the opposite side of Pakistan from India, Pakistan’s army claimed that India was supporting the insurgents, an allegation denied by India.
Munir has reiterated his country’s traditional position on Kashmir, supporting self-determination for the people of the region. He has vowed that Kashmir will one day become part of Pakistan and has referred to Kashmir as Pakistan’s “jugular vein.” In April 2025 fresh tensions between India and Pakistan erupted after a terrorist attack in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir, killed 26 people, mostly tourists. India blamed Pakistan for facilitating the attack, citing a history of supporting insurgency in the region and its alleged support for previous terrorist attacks against Indian civilians and soldiers. Pakistan rejected the accusations, claiming the group that India accused of orchestrating the attack was defunct and calling for an independent investigation. As tensions escalated between the two countries, Munir warned that Pakistan would retaliate swiftly to any Indian military action. On May 7, 2025, India launched multiple missile strikes on what it said were militant targets in Pakistan. This led to a sharp escalation, with exchanges from both sides, before a ceasefire was eventually agreed to.

articles.title: Industry seeks extension of PLI scheme for white goods: EPACK Durable MD - electronics.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.summary: Industry seeks extension of PLI scheme for white goods: EPACK Durable MD  electronics.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: A top executive at homegrown EPACK Durable said the consumer durables makers have sought an extension of the production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme for white goods, as revenue threshold was too stringent.Ajay DD Singhania, managing director (MD), EPACK Durable, told ETElectronicsWorld in an interview.
The government had envisioned a fivefold jump in revenue in the fourth year under the scheme, which has not yet materialised, Singhania said. “Each investment has a cycle, and revenue generation takes time…many people could not take advantage despite having invested.”
The PLI scheme for white goods has an outlay of ₹6,238 crore, with an implementation timeline from FY2021-22 to FY2028-29. It provides a 4-6% financial incentive on the incremental sales of locally manufactured components over a baseline year, and envisions increasing domestic value addition from 15-20% to 75-80%.
“The government is still left with a substantial budget…," he said, underscoring that the industry together with EPACK Durable has recommended the government to extend the PLI for 2-3 years more.
Till now, it has attracted an investment commitment of ₹11,198 crore from 85 approved beneficiaries, which is expected to lead to an expected production value of ₹1.90 lakh crore during the scheme period.
EPACK Durable says it is the second-largest room air conditioner (RAC) original design manufacturer (ODM) in India. It manufactures fully assembled ACs, including indoor and outdoor units, and window ACs, as well as RAC components for various brands such as Voltas, Blue Star, Haier Appliances India, Carrier Midea India, Havells India, Godrej & Boyce, and supplies components to LG Electronics India.
“We have formed a technology joint venture (JV) with China’s Hisense, wherein we are bringing Hisense's global tech products to India, including a front-load washing machine,” Singhania said, adding that Hisense launched domestically made ACs in January this year.
The listed company reported a 34% year-on-year increase in the Q1FY27 revenue to ₹886 crore, supported by broad-based growth across its portfolio.
The company, during a post-earnings conference call with analysts, said that EPACK’s core RAC business continued to grow strongly, while small and large domestic appliances as well as components scaled up at an “encouraging pace”, led by air fryers and washing machines.

articles.title: India must link industrial support to export competitiveness amid global supply shocks: CEA Nageswaran - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: India must link industrial support to export competitiveness amid global supply shocks: CEA Nageswaran  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
Chief Economic Advisor V Anantha Nageswaran on Thursday called for a shift in India's industrial strategy, saying support for domestic manufacturing must be linked to export competitiveness and the ability to match import prices, as global supply disruptions make access to critical resources increasingly uncertain.
Speaking at the ISID-IDRA Fourth National Conference during the inaugural session, Nageswaran said the country could no longer rely on markets to provide essential goods as smoothly as during the decades before the pandemic.
He said governments and industries must focus on building domestic capabilities and reducing dependence on supplies that could be restricted during geopolitical tensions.
Nageswaran said India's approach to import substitution must differ from earlier strategies and require industries to demonstrate stronger competitiveness. "So in other words, we have to insist on quid pro quo from the industry in terms of export competitiveness, and or import parity," he said.
He also cautioned that protection without investment to improve productivity could weaken industrial resilience. The presentation accompanying his remarks called for time-bound support linked to performance and exports, with protection withdrawn once domestic capacity becomes competitive.
The remarks come as India records strong economic and manufacturing growth amid global uncertainty. He cited real GDP growth of 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of 2026-27, manufacturing gross value added growth of 9.2 per cent and gross fixed capital formation growth of 11.9 per cent.
However, manufacturing's share of gross value added remained broadly unchanged at 14.8 per cent in 2025-26, compared with 14.7 per cent in 2022-23. The presentation also showed that core merchandise imports rose 19.7 per cent year-on-year during April-September 2026, faster than the 16.2 per cent growth in core exports.
"Last six years have seen many shocks with one common element - supply side shocks; semiconductor chip shortages, tariffs linked trade retaliation, vulnerability to crude oil", Nageswaran said.
He further added that conventional monetary and fiscal responses were less effective when the problem was a shortage of goods rather than weak demand.
"Monetary policy will be much more difficult to implement in a world of supply shocks," he said, adding that fiscal support would be more effective when directed towards production and productivity.
He also stressed the need to build buffers of essential commodities and strengthen domestic manufacturing so India can withstand external disruptions and become a more important supplier to global markets. (ANI)

articles.title: Albanese presses lawmakers to pass the EU trade deal, saying it would free 98% of exports from tariffs - Vinetur
articles.summary: Albanese presses lawmakers to pass the EU trade deal, saying it would free 98% of exports from tariffs  Vinetur
articles.full_text:
He said the pact would add A$10 billion to the economy, expanding market access for beef, wine, minerals and services
Thursday, October 29, 2026
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese used a press conference at Parliament House on Thursday, October 29, to press lawmakers to back legislation needed to put Australia’s trade agreement with the European Union into effect, arguing that the deal would widen market access for exporters at a time of rising global pressure on free trade.
Albanese said the agreement would make 98% of Australian exports of goods and services tariff-free in the EU, which he described as a market of 450 million people, and would add A$10 billion to the Australian economy. He said the gains would extend across critical minerals, services, manufacturing, fruit and vegetables, and wine, and would also increase access for beef and sheep meat exports.
“This is a good deal for Australia,” Albanese said, adding that failure to pass it would leave Australia at a disadvantage against countries that already have trade arrangements with the bloc, including New Zealand. He said that if Australia “shut ourselves out of this,” competing exporters would gain a comparative advantage in Europe.
The European agreement has become a political issue in Canberra as the government seeks parliamentary support for a wider economic agenda. Albanese said the deal was “front and centre” for the government even though the enabling measures were not being voted on during the final days of this week’s parliamentary sitting. He urged lawmakers to treat the agreement as a national economic priority.
According to Albanese, Coalition critics have argued that the agreement is a poor deal and objected to its climate language. He rejected both points, saying the government had previously walked away from an earlier version, returned to negotiations, and secured better terms. He also said references to the Paris climate agreement were not unusual, noting that climate provisions also appear in trade agreements with the United Kingdom, the United States, and China.
Albanese said the agreement would expand current access for red meat exporters, stating that sheep meat and beef quotas would rise to four and eight times current export levels, respectively, with a review after five years and the possibility of further increases. He also pointed to the government’s handling of geographical naming issues, citing feta as an example of a concern that had been addressed.
The issue matters beyond agriculture and heavy industry. If the agreement is implemented, it could improve Australian wine producers’ access to Europe while also opening the Australian market further to European products. That has the potential to alter competition and pricing across parts of the beverage sector, especially for wine, even as the exact commercial effects would depend on how producers and importers respond.
Albanese said cheaper imports under the agreement would help put downward pressure on prices for Australian consumers. He framed that argument within a broader defense of trade liberalization, saying Australia should present itself in global forums as a country that supports “free and fair trade unequivocally.”
His push on the EU deal came alongside other major items on the government’s parliamentary agenda. Albanese said the House of Representatives had passed the government’s Digital Duty of Care legislation on Wednesday, October 28, and called on the Senate to approve it. He said the bill would make large technology companies more accountable for content carried on their platforms and give users greater control over the material they receive through algorithms.
He also said tax legislation would be taken up on Thursday, October 29, describing it as part of a broader effort to align taxation of labor income and asset income more closely. Albanese acknowledged that tax reform is difficult and said the government had already adjusted measures through consultation, but he maintained that the overall approach was necessary to avoid placing more of the tax burden on wage earners.
Another major vote on Thursday, October 29, concerned the government’s domestic gas reservation package. Standing with Resources Minister Madeleine King, Industry Minister Tim Ayres, and Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, Albanese said the bill would allow the government to reserve up to 20% of gas exports for domestic use. He said that would increase supply for Australian manufacturers and help reduce domestic prices.
King called the package a “landmark” reform and said it would create a long-term framework for households, businesses, manufacturers, and the gas industry. Ayres said the measure went directly to Australia’s industrial competitiveness and would help secure heavy industrial jobs in outer suburbs and regional areas. Bowen said Australia was unusual among major gas-producing countries in not having an effective reservation policy and said the legislation would change that.
The government’s trade and energy messages were closely tied to cost-of-living concerns that dominated several questions at the press conference. Albanese said households were still facing pressure from inflation and the risk of further interest-rate increases, and he argued that the government’s strategy combined budget restraint with targeted measures such as free technical education, cheaper medicines, and health spending.
He said global factors remained central to the inflation outlook, pointing to higher oil prices and conflict in the Middle East. Those pressures, he said, were feeding through not only into fuel costs but also into the price of goods transported across the economy.
Albanese also used the appearance to place the trade push in a broader international context. He said he would attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in November and would use overseas meetings to advance Australia’s economic and diplomatic priorities, including trade and its campaign for a United Nations Security Council seat.
When asked about criticism from within the opposition’s ranks, Albanese said it was surprising that support for freer trade was being questioned in a party that has long presented itself as market-oriented. He warned that resistance to the EU agreement would move Australian politics toward protectionism at a moment when trade barriers are becoming a larger issue internationally.
Albanese said the debate was especially important because the global trade environment has become more uncertain. He argued that Australia’s growth and productivity depend on international engagement and said the EU agreement should be seen in the same context as the government’s earlier trade efforts with the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, and Southeast Asia.

articles.title: India, Mexico formally begin preferential trade agreement negotiations - Business Standard
articles.summary: India, Mexico formally begin preferential trade agreement negotiations  Business Standard
articles.full_text:
India, Mexico formally begin preferential trade agreement negotiations
The proposed agreement will cover market access, rules of origin, customs procedures and trade remedies as India looks to deepen its trade footprint in Latin America
Listen to This Article
India and Mexico have launched negotiations for a preferential trade agreement (PTA) after signing the terms of reference (ToR) for the proposed deal, the Department of Commerce said on Wednesday.
“The signing formally launches negotiations for a mutually beneficial and balanced PTA, with the potential to expand bilateral trade, create business opportunities, enhance investment flows and contribute to resilient and diversified supply chains,” the department said in a press release.
The signing of the ToR and launch of negotiations were part of Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal’s two-day visit to Mexico City, which began on Tuesday.
The two sides had finalised the ToR more than three months ago and were awaiting an appropriate time to schedule the visit and formal signing.
“During the visit of Commerce Secretary, Rajesh Agrawal, both delegations discussed bilateral relations and opportunities to expand trade and investment flows,” the release said.
Also Read
“The discussions were held with Mexico’s Undersecretary of Foreign Trade, Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez Romano, who participated on behalf of Secretary of Economy Marcelo Ebrard Casaubon.”
The ToR for a trade agreement serves as a formal roadmap setting out the boundaries, objectives, scope and rules before official negotiations begin.
The India-Mexico ToR covers key negotiating areas, including market access for goods, rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, dispute settlement, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade and trade remedies.
The proposed deal seeks to leverage complementarities between the two economies and expand opportunities for Mexican products and businesses in the Indian market.
“With its strong linkages to global value chains, Mexico is an important market for Indian exporters and investors. Sectors with significant potential for cooperation include automotive, chemicals, electronics, pharmaceuticals, agri-food, energy, critical minerals, medical devices, and advanced manufacturing, among others,” the release said.
New Delhi initiated discussions for a trade agreement with Mexico after the latter imposed tariffs of as much as 50 per cent on more than 1,400 products from non-preferential trading partners, including India.
Despite the tariffs, India’s exports to Mexico have grown nearly 26 per cent so far in the current financial year through August, according to the latest data available with the Department of Commerce.
India exported goods worth $5.73 billion to Mexico in 2025-26 (FY26), with nearly half of the shipments comprising vehicles and auto components, and electrical machinery and equipment.
India recorded a trade surplus of $3.63 billion with Mexico during the year.
The proposed agreement with Mexico is part of India’s broader strategy to diversify export markets and expand its footprint in Latin America.
The Department of Commerce is also engaged in trade agreement negotiations with other economies in the region, including Chile and Peru, as well as the Brazil-led five-member Mercosur bloc.

articles.title: Section 338 Canada List Adds About 100 Tariff Lines Starting October 30; Carriers Deploy Record Capacity on TPEB Over Golden Week - Flexport
articles.summary: Section 338 Canada List Adds About 100 Tariff Lines Starting October 30; Carriers Deploy Record Capacity on TPEB Over Golden Week  Flexport
articles.full_text:
Logistics Update
Trends to Watch
Talking Tariffs
- Section 338 Product List for Canada Gets Reshuffled Again, With New Duties Starting October 30: An October 23 presidential action changes which Canadian goods face Section 338 duties, and the new list applies to entries on or after October 30. A total of 22 tariff lines come off, among them plywood, plastic wrap, cardboard boxes, and food-related machinery, while about 100 go on, including cocoa products, carpets and other floor coverings, wood panels, coatings, air conditioning units, and some recreational goods.
  - The timing matters for anything in transit: a chest-type freezer, for example, owes only Section 232 steel duties on entries through October 29 and then picks up Section 338 duties on top beginning October 30, while plywood moves the other way and stops attracting the 50% Section 338 rate after October 29, per Flexport’s Tariff Simulator.
  - The duties stack on top of Section 232 tariffs and apply whether or not a product qualifies for U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) treatment.
  - This is the second round of list changes since mid-September, when cheese, hides, motorboats, and other items were added and a few large-format spirits were dropped. It also lands while the first lawsuit challenging the tariffs works its way through the Court of International Trade.
  - Importers moving Canadian-origin goods should re-run classification against the new annex before shipments land, since the list has shifted in both directions. The Tariff Simulator already reflects the updated product list.
- Wind Turbines Get a Negotiation Track Rather Than New Section 232 Tariffs: An October 22 proclamation closes out the Section 232 investigation into wind turbines without adding a new tariff. The Commerce Department found that turbines and their components pose a national security risk, citing remote-access weaknesses in imported inverters, radar interference, and strain on the electrical grid, and President Donald Trump agreed, but he directed Commerce and the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) to negotiate with trading partners and report back within 180 days instead of imposing duties.
  - Existing Section 232 duties aren’t touched. Turbine components made of steel, aluminum, or copper still pay the tariffs already in place on those metals, and the proclamation states that it doesn’t modify them.
  - Other remedies stay available depending on how the negotiations go, and the 180-day update comes due around April 20, 2027.
  - Importers of turbines and turbine components should keep classification and metal-content records current, since the existing metals duties continue to apply to those parts in the meantime.
- Robotics and Industrial Machinery Imports Get a Negotiation Mandate Instead of Tariffs, With a 180-Day Check-In: The Section 232 investigation into robotics and industrial machinery ended with a finding but no new duties. Commerce concluded that the amount of robots, factory equipment, and parts coming in from abroad is a national security risk, and the President agreed in an October 28 proclamation, yet the remedy he chose for now is diplomacy: Commerce and USTR are to work out agreements with exporting countries and report back within 180 days.
  - Tariffs aren’t off the table for good. The proclamation says the President may revisit duties, quotas, and fees, or set up an incentive program for new U.S. production of robotics and machinery, depending on how the talks go, and he can act sooner if no agreement materializes within the 180 days.
  - The administration’s reasoning leans on import dependence and data security. The U.S. relies on foreign sources for most types of robotics and industrial equipment, and the proclamation flags cybersecurity weaknesses in imported systems that sit inside manufacturing and defense operations.
  - Importers of industrial equipment should plan around a decision window that closes in late April 2027, when the robotics update comes due, rather than assume the question is settled.
- Latest UFLPA Entity List Update Takes the Roster to 190 Companies: Screening suppliers against the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List is about to take a bit longer: the roster is heading to 190 companies, up three, after the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) named additional businesses with ties to Xinjiang in a Federal Register notice.
  - Goods made wholly or in part by a listed entity are presumed to involve forced labor and are blocked from entry unless the importer shows with clear and convincing evidence that they don’t.
  - The presumption reaches inputs as well as finished goods, so U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) can detain a shipment that contains material from a listed company several tiers upstream, even when the direct supplier isn’t on the list.
  - Importers should screen their supplier and sub-tier supplier lists against the updated roster now. The Federal Register notice carries the three added names and their effective date, and Flexport’s Trade Advisory group can help importers work through a UFLPA detention if one occurs.
TRANS-PACIFIC EASTBOUND (TPEB)
- Capacity and Demand:
  - Carriers deployed record capacity during Golden Week, with weekly Asia-to-U.S. West Coast capacity at 393,000 TEU compared with a normal level below 300,000 TEU.
  - Delayed vessels bunched together and sailed as “double sailings,” which canceled out planned blank sailings.
  - With the winter slack season starting, carriers are matching capacity to softer demand to protect rates, rather than responding to a demand-driven squeeze.
- Freight Rates:
  - Trans-Pacific rates remain above Asia-Europe levels, but the planned November 1 rate increase faces pressure as carriers compete for volume.
  - The U.S. has also proposed extending its suspension of added port fees on China-linked vessels to January 9, 2027. The current suspension expires November 10.
  - Shippers should add buffer to cargo-ready dates out of Shanghai and Ningbo for the next few weeks and avoid relying on a single sailing.
FAR EAST WESTBOUND (FEWB)
- Capacity and Demand:
  - Blank sailings are 8.1% this week, with 3.4% next week and a range of 4.8-11.4% through November.
  - Overall deployed capacity to Northern Europe is still expected to reach a record level, so the blanks reflect carriers managing utilization against excess supply, rather than a space shortage.
- Suez Canal Return:
  - Capacity continues to shift back to standard Suez Canal routing. About 63% of Far East-to-Europe deployed capacity now sails via Suez: 70% on Far East to Mediterranean and 58% on Far East to Northern Europe.
  - MSC resumed Suez transits in August. The Gemini Cooperation of Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd began returning services in Q3, and Maersk aims to return all services by March 2027.
  - CMA CGM kept a Suez presence throughout, and Ocean Alliance has restored 6 services.
  - Premier Alliance has announced returns, while ZIM has not resumed. Some carriers keep selected Cape of Good Hope services as a hedge.
  - Shorter transit times are an option on part of the network, though the shift is happening carrier by carrier, even vessel by vessel, so shippers should confirm routing at booking.
  - Ships returning to Suez are also arriving alongside vessels still sailing around the Cape, which adds port congestion.
- Freight Rates:
  - Rates on the main Shanghai-to-Northern Europe index were unchanged week over week.
  - Carriers’ November 1 rate increase is unlikely to hold as supply outpaces demand. The situation will continue to be monitored.
TRANS-ATLANTIC WESTBOUND (TAWB)
- Capacity and Demand:
  - Blank sailings are 7.9% this week, then range from 0% to ~9% over the next 4 weeks. Offered capacity stays 5-16% below standard in most weeks, and selective NEUR-US East/Gulf blanks continue (~5% cancellations).
  - Vessel utilization is above 93% out of NEUR and WMED, so capacity is largely deployed.
- Operations:
  - Schedule reliability for the largest carrier networks was only 68-69% in August and September, against a 90% goal for the largest network.
  - Yards remain tight in Rotterdam, Bremerhaven and Hamburg, and container/chassis availability is limited at inland origins. Shippers should book 3-4 weeks ahead and build extra time between cargo-ready dates and vessel cutoffs.
- Freight Rates:
  - The winter slack season and added capacity from the Suez return point to continued pressure on rates. The Suez return is gradual and partial, so the effect on TAWB is likely indirect and slower than on Asia-Europe.
  - The situation will continue to be monitored.
INDIAN SUBCONTINENT TO NORTH AMERICA
- Capacity and Demand:
  - The Indian Subcontinent to the US extended Peak Season is experiencing downward market pressure leading into the Diwali Holiday in India in November.
  - Port congestion and vessel bunching across South and Southeast Asia continue to absorb effective capacity but have shown improvement at key regional hubs Nhava Sheva, Colombo, and Mundra.
  - Space on the major service strings ISC to USEC has begun to become more available.
  - Origin lead times for getting loaded on time demonstrate further normalization in the market.
  - Shippers should continue to book early, allow extra time at origin ports, and confirm routing options for urgent cargo.
- Freight Rates:
  - Market rate levels have reduced for back-to-back validity periods for major lanes ISC to USEC, and rates ISC to the WC have begun to soften.

  - West Coast demand shows no sign of fading, with AI-related cargo the main driver, and rates there moved to a higher level this week.
  - Midwest and East Coast rates eased for the first time after weeks of tight space at ORD, DFW, and ATL. ATL, DFW, and MIA are the exceptions, with demand and rates holding.

articles.title: India-US Trade Agreement in Final Stages, but Challenges Remain, Jaishankar Says - INDIA New England News
articles.summary: India-US Trade Agreement in Final Stages, but Challenges Remain, Jaishankar Says  INDIA New England News
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI — India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said Thursday that negotiations over a proposed trade agreement between India and the United States have entered their final stages, although unresolved issues remain and a deal cannot be considered complete until both sides formally reach an agreement.
Speaking at the NDTV World Summit in New Delhi, Jaishankar described the negotiations as being in the “last mile,” reflecting growing expectations that the two countries are approaching a breakthrough in their long-running trade discussions.
He said recent statements by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal also suggested that the negotiations were nearing completion.
“What you’ve heard not just from Secretary Rubio, but from Minister Piyush Goyal, from others, from me, is that we are moving towards it,” Jaishankar said.
However, he cautioned against assuming that an agreement was inevitable before the remaining differences were resolved.
“Well, look, it’s never done till it’s done,” he said.
Jaishankar acknowledged that the final stages of trade negotiations can be particularly difficult, even when the parties have reached broad agreement on major issues.
“Often the last mile or the penultimate miles do pose their challenges. I think the [negotiating] teams are working through them now,” he said.
When asked about the specific obstacles preventing a final agreement, the foreign minister declined to disclose details, emphasizing that resolving those differences was the responsibility of the negotiating teams.
“If you’re asking me to tell you what exactly those challenges are, I’m sorry I won’t. That’s for the negotiators to sort out,” he added.
The comments come amid renewed diplomatic engagement between New Delhi and Washington, with senior officials from both countries expressing optimism about strengthening economic ties.
A bilateral trade agreement is widely viewed as an important step toward expanding commercial relations between the world’s two largest democracies.
Both governments have been working to deepen cooperation in areas including trade, energy, technology and defense, while addressing longstanding commercial differences.
Jaishankar’s remarks followed his recent meeting with Rubio in Mumbai, where the two leaders discussed bilateral priorities and regional developments.
According to the U.S. State Department, the talks included energy security, defense cooperation and developments in West Asia.
“The secretary reiterated that increased energy trade with the United States can play a transformative role in diversifying India’s supply chains while meeting its sizable consumer demand,” the State Department said.
Rubio also welcomed progress in bilateral defense and civil nuclear cooperation and encouraged India to increase purchases of American technology and defense systems.
The discussions underscored Washington’s interest in expanding its role as a supplier of energy, advanced technologies and defense equipment to India.
U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, who attended the meeting, described the discussions as “productive” and highlighted the growing momentum behind cooperation in several strategic sectors.
Gor said the talks focused on strengthening ties in defense, energy, emerging technologies and trade as the two countries seek to advance their broader strategic partnership.
The renewed diplomatic activity has added to expectations that a trade agreement could be finalized soon, although neither government has announced a signing date.
Jaishankar’s comments suggest that while negotiations have made substantial progress, both sides remain focused on resolving outstanding differences before making a formal announcement.
For now, the Indian government maintains that the agreement is moving closer to completion, with negotiators continuing their efforts to bridge the remaining gaps. (Source: IANS)

articles.title: Chile urges U.S. to widen tariff exemptions on exports hit by a 12.5% surcharge - Vinetur
articles.summary: Chile urges U.S. to widen tariff exemptions on exports hit by a 12.5% surcharge  Vinetur
articles.full_text:
The latest talks ended without a deal, leaving wine producers and other exporters exposed to higher costs
Friday, October 30, 2026
Chile’s government said it met with the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative on Thursday, October 29, to press for broader exemptions from a 12.5% tariff surcharge that is affecting part of the country’s exports to the United States.
The meeting brought together Paula Estévez, Chile’s undersecretary for international economic relations, and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer during Estévez’s visit to the United States. According to the Chilean government, she used the talks to restate Chile’s case for removing more products from the surcharge and to push for trading conditions that support bilateral commerce.
Chile said products that are already exempt account for 53.6% of the country’s shipments, but Santiago wants that share to grow. No new tariff agreement was announced after the meeting, and the negotiations remain open.
The latest talks are part of a longer bilateral effort that Chile says has been underway since the first half of 2025, after the Trump administration’s initial tariff announcements. Chile’s goal since then has been to preserve the best possible access for its exporters to the U.S. market, which officials describe as one of the country’s most important overseas destinations.
In comments released by the Chilean government, Estévez said the United States had changed its trade policy and was now negotiating bilateral arrangements with several countries after imposing tariffs on all of its trading partners. She said Chile was acting pragmatically to secure the best conditions it could for local exporters.
Estévez also said the Thursday, October 29, meeting was useful because it allowed Chile to reinforce its position directly with U.S. officials. She repeated Chile’s opposition to tariffs and said more Chilean products should be exempt. She added that Chile remained open to what she described as a pragmatic, mutually beneficial solution.
The meeting followed the most recent previous negotiating round in August, when a U.S. delegation led by Deputy USTR Jeffrey Goettman traveled to Chile. The October 29 contact signaled that both sides are still engaged, even though they have not yet announced a breakthrough.
The tariff dispute matters beyond Chile’s broader export sector because any expansion of exemptions could have direct effects on beverage trade. Wine is among the Chilean products exposed to the 12.5% surcharge, and any relief would likely improve the position of Chilean producers in the U.S. market. Lower duties could also change competitive conditions among imported wines and other beverage categories by affecting retail pricing, margins, and the relative appeal of different origins.
That makes the talks especially important for Chile’s wine industry, which relies heavily on export markets and has long treated the United States as a key destination. For importers, distributors, and retailers in the U.S., the outcome could influence sourcing decisions if tariff costs remain in place or are reduced for some products and not for others.
The Chilean government did not provide a detailed list of the products discussed in the latest meeting, nor did it say whether the two sides had narrowed their differences on specific goods. Its statement focused instead on Chile’s general effort to widen the pool of exempt products and maintain favorable access to the American market.
The October 29 meeting took place during a U.S. visit linked to the program “Navigating the Global Trade Reset: Strategic Options for Latin America and the Caribbean,” organized by the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean and the Georgetown Americas Institute. Chile said the trip also included meetings with other U.S. officials on the broader economic relationship between the two countries.
According to the Chilean government, Estévez’s agenda in the United States included talks with Juan Pablo Segura at the State Department and with senior Commerce Department officials responsible for industry and security and for international trade. Those meetings also centered on economic ties between Chile and the United States, underscoring that the tariff issue is being handled alongside a wider set of commercial and strategic discussions.

articles.title: UK-India trade pact to deepen manufacturing ties: Mark Birrell, trade counsellor, British High Commission to.. - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: UK-India trade pact to deepen manufacturing ties: Mark Birrell, trade counsellor, British High Commission to..  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
CETA aims to boost technology sharing, engineering services and supply-chain partnerships beyond tariff cuts, with the UK seeking to translate improved market access into commercial deals.
Speaking on the sidelines of the first business activation of the CETA Marketplace between the two countries, held recently in Mumbai, Birrell said the agreement would make cross-border trade easier and help businesses explore new commercial opportunities.
“We are really excited about CETA because it makes a difference to UK and Indian companies. It’s not just about tariffs coming down, even though that’s very important. It’s about products and services becoming cheaper, easier and quicker to trade across the two countries,” Birrell said.
As far as manufacturers are concerned, the opportunity exists not just in the exporting of their goods at lower prices but in partnering with entities who can help them enhance their market position.
Advanced manufacturing in focus
The manufacturing opportunity was reflected in the Marketplace’s dedicated zone for advanced manufacturing, automotive and aerospace. Participating companies included Rolls-Royce, Aston Martin, Bentley, Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), Unipart Services India, Peel Ports and ISS Airview.
The presence of companies from these sectors brought an industrial dimension to the business activation, creating an opportunity for discussions with Indian companies and investors about potential areas of cooperation.
For Indian manufacturers, such engagement could open doors to exploring partnerships with some of the leading British businesses in engineering, industrial services and technology. As for UK businesses, they could make use of the platform to scout for potential Indian business partners and gain knowledge of the local market environment.
Why the agreement matters beyond tariffs
Birrell said CETA’s benefits extended beyond the movement of goods, with provisions relating to services, mobility and intellectual property creating scope for businesses to develop new partnerships.
“Alongside tariffs coming down for goods, the deal benefits services trade as well. There are provisions regarding mobility and intellectual property, which would help firms collaborate with each other in forming new partnerships,” he added.
For manufacturing firms, this wider context is significant since the competitiveness of industrialisation is not only based on the costs of production and exports. Engineering know-how, technical support, intellectual property, and technology could be some of the areas that can be applied in product development and manufacturing.
The pact could thus encourage Indian and UK firms to transcend from traditional buyer-supplier relationships to joint ventures, technology development and integration of supply chains. But the level of this type of cooperation will be determined by the economic interest of particular companies, as well as the capacity to develop viable ventures. While the agreement sets the stage for such cooperation, the actual development of new ventures will depend on further business decisions.
Birrell also mentioned the “UK-Maharashtra Growth Partnership,” which was signed during the visit of the UK Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Jonathan Reynolds and the Chief Minister of Maharashtra, Devendra Fadnavis, as another example of efforts made towards turning the trade ties into state-level engagement.
"That is one way of how we are going about it right now: taking the deal to the next level by implementing it in companies and states like Maharashtra to ensure that everybody wins," he explained.
As far as manufacturers are concerned, state-level involvement may facilitate trade and industry linkages.
Understanding the rules of market access
While lower tariffs can improve the commercial case for exports, businesses still need to understand the requirements for entering a new market and qualifying for preferential treatment.
Product standards, certification, customs documentation and rules of origin remain important considerations for manufacturers assessing the agreement’s relevance to their operations.
Birrell said CETA was intended to simplify trade and ease some of the barriers businesses face when operating across borders.
“The important thing about CETA is that it makes trade simpler. Non-tariff barriers are coming down, and regulatory and compliance requirements should be easier than before the trade deal,” he said.
As for manufacturers, knowing which provisions apply to their products will be crucial when estimating the cost of exporting, pricing policy and possible profits from entering the other market.
Converting business discussions into fruitful outcomes
The opportunity now is to convert interest in the agreement into business relationships that deliver tangible results.
Birrell said the UK government wanted companies to make practical use of CETA rather than treat it simply as a trade framework.
“Our goal as the UK government now is to make sure that CETA is utilised to its maximum effect. That means taking what is written on paper and making it real in the real world,” he said.
The Marketplace was organised to bring innovative British companies into direct contact with Indian businesses, investors and other stakeholders, allowing them to showcase their offerings and explore specific areas of cooperation.
“By doing this, we’re getting into deal-level discussions and making specific partnerships and collaborations,” Birrell said.

Goyal expressed confidence that when the details of the deal are released, the people of India will recognise that the sensitive interests of farmers and other stakeholders have not been compromised and that India will be placed at a strong comparative advantage.
He said that the opposition parties who are criticising the agreement lack understanding and knowledge about the subject.
Goyal expressed confidence that when the details of the deal are released, the people of India will recognise that the sensitive interests of farmers and other stakeholders have not been compromised and that India will be placed at a strong comparative advantage.
"The US free trade deal is sometimes sought to be politicised by a few elements... because of lack of understanding and lack of knowledge. Details are not yet fully out...I do not know what they (opposition parties) criticise.
Congress has raised concerns on multiple occasions over the deal. It has demanded that the India-US interim trade agreement be put on hold.
India and the US, in February, announced finalisation of the framework for the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement (BTA). However, changes in the tariff landscape in the US have led to further negotiations on the pact.
India is seeking lower tariffs for its goods in the US market than its competitor nations such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia.
The minister added that trade is fundamentally about comparative advantage and competitiveness, rather than absolute numbers alone.
Many developed countries had structured their tariff schedules to impose high duties on labour-intensive goods, using them as negotiating instruments, he said.
Goyal also said that India walked out of the RCEP (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership) agreement as it would have severely impacted India's manufacturing sector.
India, in November 2019, decided not to join the mega free trade agreement RCEP as the pact was not addressing its concerns.
The RCEP members included 10 ASEAN members (Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam) and their six free-trade pact partners: Australia, China, India, Japan, South Korea and New Zealand.
RCEP would have been a death knell for manufacturing in India, he said, adding that the pact could have turned India into "a nation of salesmen and salesgirls, marketing Chinese goods in India".
Further, Goyal said that quality, global market access, economies of scale and inclusivity are four key differentiators that would accelerate the transformation of India's industrial landscape.
With markets opening across the world through free trade agreements, India must compete for market share, expand its global presence and leverage preferential market access, he said.
He added that the country's trade agreements were not limited to reducing tariffs, framing rules of origin or securing market access.
They were comprehensive partnerships that considered India's competitive strengths, identified opportunities for exports, protected sensitive sectors and facilitated access to high-technology products, graphics processing units (GPUs), memory technology, medical technology and other goods required for development, Goyal said.
He also said that the nine free trade and bilateral trade agreements finalised by the government had opened up preferential market opportunities in economies with an aggregate GDP of $60 trillion, compared with $10 trillion covered by agreements concluded before 2014.
He said that the earlier agreements were largely with countries competing with India, whereas the current approach sought to foster complementary economic relationships. The minister highlighted the growing international recognition of Indian talent and skills.
Recalling a conversation with the German foreign minister regarding the migration agreement between India and Germany and the requirement for 90,000 Indians annually, Goyal said that he was told Germany needed substantially more Indian talent.
He cited the presence of Indian professionals in senior positions at Fortune 500 companies and among developers of cutting-edge technologies as evidence of the capabilities of India's workforce.
On climate change, he stressed that climate actions must be guided by the 'polluter pays principle' and 'common but differentiated responsibilities', with adequate financial and technological support for developing countries.
He highlighted that 60 per cent of India's installed electricity capacity came from green and renewable sources, while coal remained essential for energy security and affordable power.

articles.title: Trump administration to deport 150 Afghan refugees to Afghanistan via Pakistan - The Times of India
articles.summary: Trump administration to deport 150 Afghan refugees to Afghanistan via Pakistan  The Times of IndiaU.S. to Send Dozens Back to Afghanistan, Despite Risk of Persecution  The New York TimesTrump administration plans to deport some Afghan immigrants to Afghanistan  Deccan HeraldUS to deport over 150 Afghans via Pak despite persecution risk under Taliban: Report  India TodayAfghans scheduled for deportation may include relatives of those who worked alongside US...
articles.full_text:
The Trump administration is preparing to deport more than 150 Afghan immigrants and refugees to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan via Pakistan. The first deportation flight could take off as early as Monday.
The broader plan reportedly involves routing deportees through Pakistan because the United States has no diplomatic relations with the Taliban government in Afghanistan.
According to NBC News, Shawn VanDiver, president of San Diego-based advocacy group AfghanEvac, said at least 80 Afghans had recently been transferred to Louisiana from 34 ICE detention facilities across the United States. Of those, 19 were reportedly moved without legal representation.
Many of those facing deportation reportedly fled Afghanistan following the Taliban's return to power in 2021, including individuals whose family members had worked alongside US forces during the two-decade war.
Shawn warned that returning these individuals could expose them and their families to serious risks of persecution and retaliation.
"Some facing deportation are brothers and sons of men who served alongside US forces, families the Taliban already has every reason to target," VanDiver added.
A senior Trump administration official, speaking anonymously to NBC News, indicated that the potential consequences for Afghans facing deportation were not a major concern for the White House. “The administration’s position is, ‘These individuals do not have status in our country, therefore we don’t really care what happens to them,’” the official said.
The proposed removals come amid US president Donald Trump's broader immigration crackdown. Since returning to office, his administration has suspended refugee admissions, including those for Afghans who had sought protection in the United States following the 2021 withdrawal of US-led forces.
The policy marks a reversal of earlier efforts to provide refuge to Afghans fleeing Taliban rule and political instability.
The administration has also pursued third-country deportation arrangements, sending migrants to countries other than their countries of origin. Immigration lawyers and human rights advocates argue that such arrangements could circumvent international protections against returning asylum seekers to places where they may face persecution. The legality of these deportation policies is expected to come before the US Supreme Court in December.
VanDiver has called on Congress to intervene by passing legislation granting eligible Afghans temporary protected status (TPS), which would provide protection from deportation while conditions in Afghanistan remain dangerous.
Pakistan could also face complications if the proposed deportations proceed through its territory. Islamabad has already deported more than two million Afghan nationals since 2023.

articles.title: Column: China International Import Expo widens gateway for African products to Chinese market - India's News.Net
articles.summary: Column: China International Import Expo widens gateway for African products to Chinese market  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
by Sizo Nkala
Trade has long been an important pillar of Africa-China cooperation. As China continues to open its vast domestic market, African countries and businesses are gaining more opportunities to bring their products to Chinese consumers.
A series of measures is helping turn these opportunities into greater market access, including the zero-tariff treatment for products from 53 African countries that have diplomatic relations with China from May 1, the establishment of green channels for African agricultural products, and wider use of China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, or CIPS, by African financial institutions to lower trade transaction costs.
Such measures are designed to strengthen Africa's export capacity and competitiveness while demonstrating China's commitment to a more open, inclusive and development-oriented trade relationship with the continent.
Meanwhile, market access is meaningful only when businesses can find buyers. This makes the China International Import Expo (CIIE) an increasingly important platform for African exporters.
Launched in 2018 as the world's first national-level expo dedicated to imports, the CIIE was designed to expand China's opening-up and turn its vast market into a shared opportunity for the world.
The ninth CIIE will be held in Shanghai from Nov. 5 to 10. Preparations are basically complete. A total of 162 countries, regions and international organizations will take part, with 4,142 overseas companies exhibiting.
For African exporters, however, the significance of the CIIE lies not simply in its size, but in its ability to connect relatively small businesses with a market that may otherwise be difficult to reach.
Zambian honey, Nigerian cashew nuts, Beninese pineapples and Kenyan flowers have all made breakthroughs and secured markets in China through the CIIE. South African exporters of rooibos tea, wine, avocados, and jewelry have also secured contracts at previous editions of the expo.
South Africa's Standard Bank hosted 21 export clients at the 2025 CIIE. According to the bank, clients from four African markets secured export contracts with Chinese importers worth approximately 140 million U.S. dollars that year through its Africa-China Trade Solutions initiative.
These contracts are not just numbers. They have tangible benefits for ordinary people in Africa by creating job opportunities and thereby contributing to poverty eradication.
Another welcome development is the further upgrade of the Asia-Africa Products Zone, first introduced at last year's CIIE, with more exhibition space for African businesses this year.
To encourage greater African participation, particularly by micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), organizers will also hold a dedicated business matchmaking event for Asian and African food and agricultural products, helping connect exporters with potential Chinese buyers.
Moreover, small businesses from least developed countries, most of which are in Africa, can participate in the expo at reduced cost through free exhibition booths and other logistical and operational support. Such measures make the CIIE more inclusive and accessible, particularly for Africa's MSMEs, which account for nearly 90 percent of businesses across the continent.
By lowering the barriers to participation, the CIIE ensures that small businesses, the engines of economic growth and development in most African countries, have access to China's large import market.
For African governments and businesses, therefore, the CIIE is more than a trade fair. It is a platform through which market-opening measures can be translated into commercial opportunities.
As the ninth CIIE approaches, African exporters have another opportunity to show their presence to Chinese buyers.
Editor's note: Sizo Nkala is a senior research fellow at the University of Johannesburg's Center for Africa-China Studies.

articles.title: Trump's Russian Diesel Is a Legal Hot Potato With a Five-Year Fuse - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.summary: Trump's Russian Diesel Is a Legal Hot Potato With a Five-Year Fuse  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comRussia plans to export 2.15 million tons of diesel in November, media say  ReutersSix oil tankers carrying 268,000 tonnes of Russian diesel sail towards US  The GuardianThree Russian diesel tankers steam for US — including two under sanctions  Financial TimesTrump Aides Are Leaning on U.S. Firms to Accept Russian Diesel  NOTUS
articles.full_text:
A Malta-flagged tanker called the Agioi Fanendes left the Russian port of Primorsk on Oct. 22 carrying nearly 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low-sulfur diesel, and ship-tracking data has it arriving at the Port of New York and New Jersey on Nov. 7, four days after the midterm elections. Nobody has publicly said who bought the fuel, and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., has asked the ship’s owner to identify the buyer and everyone else involved by Oct. 31.
The cargo is the first visible piece of the deal President Donald Trump announced Oct. 9, after a call with Vladimir Putin that was supposed to be about a suspected plague case in Russia. He announced it while envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were meeting Ukrainian officials in Miami about a proposal to end the war, saying Russia would start with 300,000 tons of diesel right away and scale up from there, and as he left the White House for a campaign rally, he told reporters, “I want to thank President Putin.” Treasury issued a license authorizing the trade the same day.
Washington spent years tightening the screws on Russian energy, and Congress wrote the import ban into law in 2022, so a president thanking Putin for diesel on his way to a rally went over about as well as you’d guess. Four days later, 12 senators, six of them Republicans, wrote to Trump asking him to rescind it. Much of the debate has centered on the politics and the fallout for Ukraine, which matters, but there’s a more practical question that gets less attention: what happens when the fuel actually shows up, and can anyone take it without worrying about a knock on the door later?
What a Treasury License Can’t Do
The document doing the work is OFAC General License 135, which authorizes transactions tied to the sale, delivery, offloading, and importation of Russian-origin diesel, including into the United States, through April 7, 2027. It’s a Treasury license rather than an executive order, and that distinction carries the whole legal fight, because a license can only relax rules the executive branch wrote itself.
Most of the Russia sanctions Treasury enforces rest on emergency powers that presidents have used since 2014, and Scott Anderson, a senior editor at Lawfare and a former State Department lawyer, says Trump can almost certainly waive those at will, but the import ban is another matter. Joe Biden banned Russian oil and fuel imports by executive order in March 2022, and Congress followed later that spring with the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, which put the ban in statute for everything under Chapter 27 of the tariff schedule, diesel included. A president can lift it only if conditions are met, among them a peace deal accepted by Ukraine’s government and advance notice to Congress, and none of that has happened.
Treasury’s only public explanation so far is a post on X saying the license is consistent with earlier actions and complies with all applicable laws. Anderson says the administration has a colorable argument built on language in the 2022 act that ties it to the original executive order, but that it’s far from clear a court would accept it. The White House does have some precedent on its side, since Treasury issued a series of 30-day licenses this spring, aimed at easing prices that spiked with the Iran war, for Russian oil already loaded on ships, and they passed without much fuss, even though there’s a separate argument that Congress should have been given advance notice of licenses that significantly change Russia policy. This one runs six months and covers future shipments, which is a bigger ask.
Blumenthal put the objection more bluntly in his letter to the shipowner, writing that the president may have issued a license but “only Congress can make it legally valid.”
The license is also drawn around diesel alone, which Anderson reads as a possible nod to the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, the sanctions law Trump signed in September. That law defines crude oil in a way that leaves diesel out, so the administration can argue it isn’t working against the letter of the statute, though whether it honors the spirit is a harder question.
Who Signs for the Cargo?
Trump himself seemed to hedge on the U.S. part of the equation earlier this month, telling reporters the arrangement wasn’t really with him and was “a deal for the world,” which sits awkwardly next to a tanker steaming for New York Harbor. If the fuel does arrive, though, someone has to take title to it, a terminal has to let it dock, a bank has to move the money, and an insurer has to cover the ship, and each of them is looking at the same exposure. The White House didn’t say at the announcement who would be paying for the fuel, and the buyer of the first cargo still hasn’t surfaced.
Importing goods contrary to law carries criminal penalties under federal customs law along with civil ones, and Anderson notes that Trump could use his pardon power to shield importers from the criminal side but not the civil side, which can reach the full value of the cargo and the forfeiture of the vessel that carried it. Customs penalties can be pursued for up to five years after a shipment arrives.
That five-year window is the real answer to whether a company could get stuck after the election, because it doesn’t depend on who controls Congress, and a president who takes office in January 2029 would still have years left on the clock for a cargo that lands in November.
Lawmakers have already started building a paper trail, beginning Oct. 24 when six senators and one House member asked major banks and port authorities in Texas and New York to preserve shipping documents, contracts and communications with government officials, and three days later Blumenthal asked the ship’s owner, the Greek firm EASTMED, to identify the seller, buyer, charterer, insurer, terminal operator and distributor, and to say whether any federal agency had given it instructions. So Treasury has said yes, while the people who would have to touch the cargo are being asked to hang on to their emails.
Allies add friction of their own, since UK and EU sanctions on Russian diesel are still in force, which Clyde & Co says bars banks and insurers based there from helping with the shipment unless it’s price cap compliant, and one of the three tankers due next month, the Leruo, is sanctioned by Britain, the EU and Canada.
Arriving After the Votes Are Counted
Three tankers carrying about 140,000 metric tons are scheduled to reach U.S. ports between Nov. 7 and Nov. 11, which puts the first unloading after the polls close, though the dates have shifted from report to report. NBC News had the Agioi Fanendes closer to Nov. 10, and gCaptain retracted a story this week about a separate cargo it had expected in Norfolk on Nov. 2. Moscow is treating the shipments as routine, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying more tankers will follow regularly, and Putin’s own readout of the call described Russia as ready to supply oil and oil products to American and global markets, which is a wider offer than diesel.
Democrats have been heavy favorites to take the House, with Polymarket traders putting the odds at 93 percent earlier this month and a Senate flip at roughly 65 percent. A Democratic House would bring document requests and subpoena power, and a sweep, which would be worse for the deal, would put Senate committee chairs behind the same questions.
A new Congress wouldn’t be seated until January, though, and Trump would still hold a veto, so the midterms are better read as a pressure point than a trigger, and the opposition isn’t strictly partisan anyway. Republican Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah joined a bipartisan statement saying the imports violate the 2022 ban; Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., has promised bipartisan legislation to block Russian oil purchases; and Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker of Mississippi has predicted the imports never materialize. Trump’s answer to GOP critics has been to dismiss them as “Republicans that can’t really be serious.”
What a landed cargo does change is who can sue, since Anderson suggests competitors such as biodiesel and renewable diesel producers would likely have standing once imports actually happen. Importers have also seen how quickly this administration’s rules can move. The Graham act passed the Senate 86 to 11 and told Trump to impose new tariffs on the biggest buyers of Russian oil by Oct. 18, and on Oct. 16 he signed an executive order that put the duties on the books and waived them in the same document. New Delhi [India], October 28 (ANI): Swedish Ambassador to India Petra Menander on Wednesday expressed optimism about the expanding bilateral relationship between India and Sweden, pointing to the upcoming India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) as a primary engine to streamline business routines and expand commercial ties.
Speaking with ANI on the trajectory of bilateral relations following their recent elevation, Menander emphasised that trade simplification will play a crucial role in fulfilling shared financial targets.
'Well, I think it's booming, and I think we will be helped by the EU Free Trade Agreement that will help simplify the trade routines that we have, because one of the main objectives is to double our economic exchange until 2030,' Menander stated. 'So, full optimism ahead.'
Addressing progress on the strategic 2030 roadmap, Menander highlighted that active efforts are already underway across commercial and diplomatic channels.
'I think as you see, what we're doing today is part of the implementation of the roadmap, and tomorrow we'll do something with the companies, and then we have our political exchange going as well,' Menander noted. 'So we're in full implementation, so to speak.'
The ambassador's remarks underline a growing momentum in trade, corporate collaboration, and high-level political exchanges as both nations work toward their 2030 bilateral goals.
Earlier this month, Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal stated that he met European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic on the sidelines of the G20 Trade Ministers' Meeting here to evaluate ongoing advancements regarding the formal signing and eventual implementation of the landmark India-EU FTA.
In addition to evaluating the bilateral trade pact, Goyal noted that both leaders conferred on collaborative strides achieved through the India-EU Trade and Technology Council, necessary structural reforms within the World Trade Organisation, and mutual strategic objectives at the G20.
Sharing details of the diplomatic engagement on social media, Goyal stated in a post on X, 'Reviewed progress towards the signing and entry into force of the India-EU FTA.'
India and the European Union successfully wrapped up comprehensive negotiations for the expansive trade accord earlier this year on January 27. The milestone followed arduous talks that initially commenced back in 2007 before being officially relaunched in 2022 following a lengthy hiatus of stalled discussions.
The agreement advanced further earlier this month when the European Commission formally transmitted the text to the EU Council to secure authorisation for its signature and conclusion.
The India-EU FTA negotiations have been a key component of efforts to deepen economic ties between the two sides, with the agreement expected to provide greater market access and strengthen trade and investment flows. The India-EU FTA was jointly announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on January 27 this year during the 16th India-EU Summit in New Delhi.
The announcement followed the resumption of negotiations in 2022 after years of discussions aimed at establishing a comprehensive and balanced trade partnership between India and the European Union.
The proposed agreement assumes significance amid growing economic ties between the two regions. In 2024-25, bilateral trade in goods between India and the EU stood at USD 136.54 billion, with India's exports to the bloc valued at USD 75.85 billion and imports at USD 60.68 billion.
Trade in services between India and the European Union reached USD 83.10 billion in 2024. (ANI)
