articles.full_text:
The India-China border dispute remains one of Asia’s most dangerous unresolved geopolitical conflicts because it combines competing territorial claims, historical grievances, military rivalry and a persistent absence of trust. More than six decades after the 1962 war, the two countries have yet to agree on a common boundary across their entire Himalayan frontier. The Line of Actual Control (LAC) which separates the respective military positions continues to be interpreted differently by New Delhi and Beijing leaving vast stretches vulnerable to confrontation.
The roots of the dispute lie partly in the conflicting boundary arrangements inherited from British India. In the eastern sector, India recognises the McMahon Line drawn during the 1914 Simla Convention as its boundary with Tibet wherein China rejects its legitimacy. In the western sector the dispute centres on Aksai Chin, a strategically important region administered by China but claimed by India as part of Ladakh. The Johnson Line, one of the historical boundary proposals associated with British India placed Aksai Chin within the territory claimed by the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. Till 1947 Maharaja Hari Singh’s army manned a small military post in this largely inhabitable area.
These competing claims have produced a frontier where military presence rather than an agreed international boundary often determines the practical limits of control. India and China have established patrol routes based on their respective interpretations of the LAC resulting in overlapping areas where encounters can quickly turn confrontational. Roads, military posts, surveillance systems and forward deployments have further intensified this competition.
The Lessons of 1962: The Disaster at Nam Ka Chu
The origins of the modern India-China confrontation can be traced to China's consolidation of control over Tibet after 1950. Tibet had historically served as a geographical buffer between the Indian subcontinent and China's political and military centres. Its incorporation into the People's Republic of China transformed the strategic environment along India's northern frontier.
The construction of a road through Aksai Chin connecting Xinjiang with western Tibet subsequently exposed the inadequacy of India's surveillance and administrative presence in the region at that time. New Delhi regarded the area as part of Ladakh while Beijing considered the road essential for integrating its western territories. The dispute over the road became one of the principal sources of tension between the two governments.
Relations deteriorated further following the Tibetan uprising of 1959 and the Dalai Lama's arrival in India. New Delhi granted him asylum, a decision taken on humanitarian grounds but viewed by Beijing through the prism of its security concerns and authority over Tibet. Border disagreements, diplomatic recriminations and mutual suspicion gradually eroded the possibility of a political settlement.
India's Forward Policy sought to reinforce its territorial claims by establishing military posts in disputed areas. The strategy was intended to prevent further Chinese consolidation without provoking a full-scale conflict. However, the deployment frequently outpaced the military infrastructure required to support it. Several posts were isolated, inadequately supplied and positioned in terrain that offered significant advantages to Chinese forces.
The Nam Ka Chu river valley in the eastern sector became the clearest illustration of these weaknesses. Indian troops were deployed below the strategically important Thagla Ridge, where Chinese forces possessed superior observation and tactical advantages. The Indian positions were difficult to reinforce as they were exposed to concentrated attacks and insufficiently supported by heavy weapons and artillery. The deployment reflected a serious mismatch between political objectives and military preparedness.
On 20th October 1962, Chinese forces launched a major offensive against Indian positions in both the eastern and western sectors. In the Nam Ka Chu valley, the exposed Indian deployment was overwhelmed by a coordinated assault. The defeat reflected not merely the numerical superiority of the attacking forces but also the consequences of poor positioning, inadequate logistics and the failure to anticipate the scale of the Chinese offensive.
The collapse of the forward positions opened the way for a wider Chinese advance into the North-East Frontier Agency, now Arunachal Pradesh. In the western sector, Chinese forces consolidated their control over Aksai Chin. Beijing announced a unilateral ceasefire in November 1962 and withdrew from much of its advance in the east but retained control over Aksai Chin.
The LAC: Competing Perceptions and Strategic Flashpoints
The LAC is not a mutually agreed international boundary. It is a military reference line whose precise alignment remains disputed across several areas. India and China patrol according to their respective perceptions of the line creating situations in which one side's routine patrol is regarded by the other as an intrusion.
This ambiguity has significant operational consequences. A patrol entering a disputed area does not automatically establish that an internationally recognised boundary has been crossed. However repeated obstruction of patrol routes, the establishment of temporary camps and the construction of permanent infrastructure can alter the practical balance on the ground. The distinction between a disputed claim and an established pattern of control consequently becomes central to the management of the frontier.
The Himalayan terrain makes the problem more complicated. High mountain passes, glaciers, river valleys and snow-covered ridges limit visibility and restrict movement. In the western sector, Ladakh has emerged as the principal theatre of military tension. The Depsang Plains are strategically important because their relatively open terrain offers access towards sensitive areas and traditional Indian patrol points. The dispute at Depsang therefore concerns not only where the LAC lies but also whether established patrol practices can continue.
Pangong Tso, a long lake extending across the frontier is particularly sensitive because the surrounding mountain spurs provide important observation points and access routes. Disagreements over patrol limits along its northern bank have repeatedly generated confrontations.
The October 2024 reaching an understanding between the Indian army and the PLA on patrolling at Depsang and Demchok represented an important step towards reducing tensions. The subsequent resumption of agreed patrolling arrangements demonstrated that negotiation could restore some previously contested activities. However, the agreement did not settle the boundary dispute or remove the broader military competition along the frontier.
In the eastern sector, China's claims over Arunachal Pradesh create a different but equally serious challenge. India regards the state as an integral part of its territory while Beijing continues to describe it as South Tibet. Tawang carries particular political and strategic significance while remote areas of Upper Subansiri and other frontier districts remain vulnerable to patrol encounters.
The December 2022 confrontation near Yangtse demonstrated that the danger extends well beyond Ladakh. Physical clashes do seldom occur particularly where both sides seek to maintain or reinforce their presence along contested ridgelines.
The recent reports in October 2026 of renewed face-offs in Upper Subansiri have raised additional concerns. Claims that Chinese personnel established tented positions six to seven kilometres inside Indian side of the LAC stems completely from the perception rather than verified territorial penetrations. Nevertheless, the broader pattern remains troubling as disputed geography, competing patrol practices and military infrastructure continue to generate confrontation in both the western and eastern sectors.

The death of a former Bangladesh Air Force officer, believed to have filmed Sheikh Hasina's flight from Dhaka, has brought his controversial past back into focus. Days after the video surfaced in August 2024, he was dismissed from service and accused of having links to India's spy agency.
Mystery surrounds the death of former Bangladesh Air Force flight lieutenant KM Tahsif Souri, who is believed to have recorded the viral video that showed former prime minister Shekh Hasina fleeing Bangladesh amid the student uprising in 2024. The discovery of Souri's body in a river in Dhaka has drawn renewed attention to his sudden exit from the Air Force and allegations of his links with India's spy agency, RAW. Months before his death, Souri addressed these issues in an explosive podcast and also questioned the government's handling of the 2025 fighter jet crash at a school that left over 35 dead.
The body of the former Bangladesh Air Force officer was found floating in the Turag River in Dhaka on October 28, over 24 hours after he went missing. Souri left his home on October 27 with a friend to repair his motorcycle but never returned. The 28-year-old's father and cousin have alleged that he was murdered, according to a report in Dhaka Tribune. While the police have remained tight-lipped, Souri's controversial past has come under renewed scrutiny.
For the report, we have scoured through past reports in Bangladeshi media and tried to piece together the circumstances in which he was dismissed from service in August 2024, days after Hasina fled to India.
THE SHEIKH HASINA VIDEO CONTROVERSY
Souri first drew public attention over his reported role in recording and circulating the footage of Hasina leaving Bangladesh on August 5, 2024. Hasina fled to India as her Awami League government collapsed amid violent student-led protests, which left over 500 dead.
The video circulated widely on social media, prompting questions about who had recorded and released it.
Interestingly, days after the video, Souri was dismissed from service in September 2024. The Bangladesh Air Force, however, said it was not linked to the recording and sharing of the Hasina video.
Souri's father said the family was told that his son was dismissed over disciplinary issues. However, the family doubted the explanation, pointing to his exemplary service record and nearly 200 hours of flying experience. His family said becoming a pilot was Souri's childhood dream.
After his dismissal, Souri worked with several organisations, including the Bangladesh Cricket Board and Netra News. He had recently started a security guard supply business.
Life had begun to return to normal for Souri before he found himself back in the headlines last year in August.
INDIA SPY ALLEGATIONS AND EXPLOSIVE PODCAST
A report published in Amar Desh, a newspaper affiliated with the Jamaat-e-Islami, identified Souri and another Air Force officer, Lieutenant Rifat Ashrafi, as the ones behind the Hasina video. The newspaper, which was shut down by the Hasina government, was relaunched in December 2024. It is owned by journalist Mahmudur Rahman.
The newspaper also alleged that an investigation into the video by the Air Force revealed links between officials within the department and India's spy agency, RAW, according to a report in bdnews24. Souri's name was among those mentioned in the report. Following this, his passport was reportedly seized by the government.
However, the allegations were swiftly rebutted by Bangladesh's Inter-Services Public Relations Directorate (ISPR). The ISPR also rejected claims that his dismissal from service was linked to a "foreign intelligence agency".
It said the two officers were retired through due process under the Air Force's existing laws and regulations under different circumstances.
Despite the ISPR statement, Souri's family claimed he was facing harassment. A colleague told Dhaka Tribune that Souri faced social pressure following the allegations in Amar Desh.
Earlier this year in July, Souri appeared in a podcast named 'Speak With Rashid'. When asked whether he lost his job in the Air Force for recording the Hasina video, Souri replied, "could be".
He also said the Amar Desh report on his alleged RAW links was nothing but propaganda. "The report Amar Desh published was actually serving some sort of propaganda," Souri said.
The former Air Force officer also raised questions about the investigation into the fighter jet crash on July 21, 2025. A Bangladesh Air Force Chengdu FT-7BGI training fighter jet crashed into the Milestone School and College campus, killing 37, including students, and leaving over 170 injured.
Souri's father, Enayetul Karim Helal, told Jago News that his son had sometimes expressed fears about his safety since the podcast went viral. "He would sometimes tell me that he was feeling a little apprehensive. But he never told me what he was worried about," Helal said.
SHEIKH HASINA'S SON RAISES QUESTIONS ON DEATH
In a hard-hitting post, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, the son of Hasina, said Souri was the victim of a propaganda campaign.
"A year earlier, Turkish citizenship holder Mahamudur Rahman's propaganda machinery labelled him as a foreign operative. In the recent podcast, the now-deceased decorated air force officer... explained how that Amar Desh-backed propaganda ruined his career and made his life miserable," Wazed tweeted.
Wazed said Souri also unravelled a series of anomalies inside the Air Force after the 2025 crash, including lack of maintenance of fighter jets.
"He also expressed fear for his life as he expressed some startling revelations inside the Air Force that often are wrapped in secrecy. He questioned the investigation surrounding the Milestone School crash, and raised doubts over the casualty toll that the Yunus regime sought to hide," he said.
Wazed also claimed that even after Souri's death, Jamaat activists doubled down on their bid to establish "Mahamudur Rahman's propaganda". "The motive behind the desperate bid to reiterate false charges involving the officer appears to be to block a fair investigation and further vilify the Awami League," he said.
WHAT WE KNOW ON SOURI'S DEATH
The sudden death of the former Air Force officer has raised considerable curiosity and intrigue.
A report in Daily Star said Souri spent most of October 27 shopping with his mother. As we have mentioned above, he later went out with his friend. He even sent his mother a message, "Mommy, I am coming". But Souri never returned.
A preliminary report said there were no injury marks on the body, but blood was coming out of his nose. The arms of the 5 ft 7 inch former officer were bent in front of his head and his fists were clenched. His abdomen was swollen, as per the report in Dhaka Tribune.
However, the exact cause of death remains unclear. Whether foul play or personal rivalry was involved will only be known once the police complete their investigation.

The two countries have signed the terms of reference (ToR) to formally launch the talks. The ToR outline broad contours of the pact.
The negotiating areas include market access for goods, rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, dispute settlement, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, technical barriers to trade and trade remedies.
It was signed in the presence of Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agarwal.
Read more: India, Mexico sign terms of reference to kickstart trade pact negotiations
Read more: India to emerge as major exporter to China, ASEAN, get edge in US trade pact, says Piyush Goyal
With its strong linkages to global value chains, Mexico is an important market for Indian exporters and investors. Sectors with significant potential for cooperation include automotive, chemicals, electronics, pharmaceuticals, agri-food, energy, critical minerals, medical devices and advanced manufacturing.
Both sides also discussed the possibility of organising a Mexican business mission to India during the first quarter of 2027. The proposed mission would facilitate business-to-business meetings, help identify commercial opportunities and strengthen commercial ties between the productive sectors of the two countries.
The bilateral trade between the two countries dipped 9.11 per cent to USD 7.83 billion (exports USD 5.72 billion and imports USD 2.1 billion) in 2025-26 as against USD 8.61 billion in 2024-25. India had a trade surplus of USD 3.62 billion in the last fiscal as against USD 2.9 billion in 2024-25.
India's major exports to Mexico include automobiles and auto components, pharmaceuticals, engineering goods and chemical products. India mainly imports crude oil, which accounts for 75 per cent of the export basket from Mexico. Other products exported to India are gold and related jewellery, chemical compounds and telephone machinery.
New Delhi is a major investor in Mexico City in sectors such as information technology, pharmaceutical and automotive sectors. Almost all major Indian IT and ICT companies (TCS, HCL, Infosys, Tech Mahindra, First Source, Cognizant, NIIT, Aptech, Hexaware, Wipro, BirlaSoft, and Zoho) have operations in Mexico.
Several Indian pharmaceutical firms (Lupin, Dr Reddy's Laboratories, Zydus, Claris, Life Sciences, Hetero Drugs, and Sun Pharma) have investments and operations in Mexico.
From the Mexican side, 17 major companies have a presence in India. Leading Mexican companies like Nemak, Metalsa, Mexichem, Great Foods & Beverages, RuhrPumpen, Cinepolis and Kidzania have invested in India in recent times.
Mexican IT company Softtek became the first Latin American company to have a presence in India as a service provider. Cinepolis has opened over 350 screens all over India, penetrating tier 2 cities as well.
India has received USD 354.44 million in foreign direct investment (FDI) from Mexico during April 2000 and June 2026.
Mexico is an important export market for India, besides a gateway to North America. A trade pact will help Indian exporters diversify trade amid global tariff uncertainty and supply-chain realignment.
The proposed preferential trade agreement (PTA) could help Indian exporters retain competitiveness, protect market access and expand business in a major Latin American economy. In a PTA, two trading partners reduce and eliminate import duties on a specified number of goods.
The PTA is also important as Mexico, from January 1 this year, steeply hiked import tariffs - ranging from about 5 per cent to as high as 50 per cent - on a wide range of goods (about 1,463 tariff lines) from countries that do not have free trade agreements with the South American nation. These countries include India, China, South Korea, Thailand and Indonesia.
The measures are expected to affect Indian products, including automobiles, textiles, footwear, chemicals and engineering goods.
According to trade experts, a PTA could secure lower duties on selected products and help Indian exporters compete with suppliers enjoying preferential access.
India has implemented seven free trade agreements with the UAE, Mauritius, Australia, the EFTA bloc, the UK, Oman and New Zealand in the last about five years. A comprehensive pact with the 27-nation European Union will be signed in December.
These pacts would help the country diversify its export basket, integrate with global supply chains and provide a cushion against escalating global trade uncertainties.

articles.title: India and Europe accelerate trade ties but investment remains the big unknown - Brussels Signal
articles.summary: India and Europe accelerate trade ties but investment remains the big unknown  Brussels Signal
articles.full_text:
India has been reshaping its trade relations with Europe amid mounting international turmoil.
As Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein mark the first anniversary of their free trade agreement with New Delhi, the European Union has completed negotiations on its own deal and is moving towards ratification.
Both developments reflect Europe’s growing interest in accessing the Indian market and in expanding its international economic relationships as the global order is reshaped. The agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which entered into force on October 1, 2025, though, still faces practical difficulties in turning commitments on paper into reality, particularly in translating greater trade openness into investment and industrial activity.
The central ambition is substantial: $100 billion (€89.8 billion) in additional investment in India over 15 years and the creation of one million direct jobs.
On October 7, during the second India-EFTA Prosperity Summit in New Delhi, both sides announced new business projects and reviewed progress under the agreement. Swiss President Guy Parmelin said that 53 companies from his country had investment plans across 20 economic sectors.
Norway, meanwhile, highlighted the presence of around 160 Norwegian companies operating in India. The governments also identified opportunities in advanced manufacturing, medical technologies, maritime transport and energy.
These announcements, though, do not yet provide a complete picture of the results. The official documentation marking the agreement’s first anniversary does not include a consolidated figure for new investment actually disbursed or jobs directly attributable to the deal. Indian government data cited by Business Standard put the increase in Swiss investment in the country at $202 million (€181 million) between September 2025 and March 2026.
Meanwhile, the European Union, which is not part of EFTA, is pursuing its own strategy.
On January 27, 2026, the European Commission and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government concluded negotiations on a much broader trade agreement. On September 11, Brussels submitted the text to the Council of the European Union to move towards its signature and approval. The agreement still needs to complete the EU’s institutional procedures, including the consent of the European Parliament, and India’s ratification process before entering into force.
The economic figures explain the interest.
According to Eurostat data published by the Council of the EU, merchandise trade between India and the EU-27 reached €118 billion in 2025. Europe imported €69.5 billion worth of Indian goods and exported €48.9 billion, resulting in a trade deficit of €20.6 billion. That made the EU India’s second-largest trading partner in goods, behind the United States and ahead of China.
In addition, the stock of European direct investment in India stood at €132.8 billion in 2024, with more than 6,000 European companies established in the country directly providing around three million jobs.
The agreement negotiated with Brussels provides for tariff reductions or eliminations covering 96.6 per cent of European goods exports to India, according to the Commission. It estimates that it could save European exporters around €4 billion annually in customs duties once fully implemented. Amid the ongoing tariff battle between Washington and Beijing, this is welcome news.
But realpolitik is stubborn and the two negotiations have followed different timelines. Talks between India and the EU resumed in 2022, before the EFTA agreement was signed. There is insufficient evidence to present Brussels’ rapprochement with New Delhi as a direct response to the deal reached by the four European countries.
The trade figures between India and EFTA reveal a deeply unbalanced relationship. During the 2025-26 financial year, which ran from April 2025 to March 2026, trade reached approximately $26.7 billion (€24 billion), with Indian exports amounting to $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) compared with imports of nearly $24.9 billion (€22.4 billion).
Gold imported from Switzerland accounts for a substantial share of this difference, meaning the deficit cannot automatically be attributed to the new agreement.
Tariff liberalisation does not eliminate regulatory obstacles either.
On July 21, during India’s eighth trade policy review at the World Trade Organization, the EU itself raised concerns over unpredictable customs procedures, complex sanitary requirements, intellectual property issues and increasing restrictions on public procurement.
Brussels also questioned certification requirements linked to certain Indian national standards, warning of “an ever-expanding number of Quality Control Orders” that risked insulating the Indian market from the world economy.
These difficulties also affect the implementation of the EFTA agreement. Although it grants preferential treatment to 99.6 per cent of the value of Indian exports to its members, smaller companies must still meet technical, documentation and quality requirements to benefit from it. The obstacle is technical and should not pose a problem in the longer term.
The investment chapter is the agreement’s most distinctive feature.
EFTA countries are required to promote an increase of $50 billion (€44.9 billion) in direct investment over the first ten years, followed by another $50 billion over the subsequent five years.
Chapter 7 of the agreement, though, establishes obligations to promote investment, not a guarantee that private companies will actually commit those amounts. India could review certain trade concessions if the targets are ultimately not met and the consultation mechanisms provided for under the agreement have been exhausted. The first formal review of progress is due within five years of entry into force and any suspension of concessions would have to be proportionate and temporary.
The agreement has allowed the four EFTA countries to move ahead of the EU in implementing preferential trade arrangements with India. Brussels has a much larger economic relationship with New Delhi, although its new agreement has yet to enter into force.
Despite the challenges, the direction of travel is encouraging. European companies are showing growing interest in India, new investment opportunities are emerging and both sides have strong incentives to deepen their economic cooperation.
The coming years will determine how quickly these opportunities translate into tangible results. But with the EFTA agreement already in operation and a broader EU-India deal moving closer to implementation, India and Europe are laying the foundations for a more ambitious economic partnership, one that could strengthen industrial cooperation, encourage technological exchange and create new opportunities for businesses on both sides.

Authored On

EU pressure on China amid a widening trade deficit and manufacturing weakness
Proposed import volume restrictions and coordination with neighboring trading partners
Mounting pressure on China to secure alternative markets to offset lost U.S. exports
Trade tensions between the European Union (EU) and China are intensifying as France and Germany, the bloc’s two central powers, pursue sweeping trade sanctions targeting China’s unfair trade practices and supply-chain distortions. Faced with a widening trade deficit and manufacturing weakness, the EU is increasing pressure through proposed import volume restrictions and calls for neighboring trading partners to coordinate their policies toward China. For China, which has expanded into other markets to circumvent U.S. tariff barriers, a contraction in access to Europe would make further export losses difficult to avoid. Rising import restrictions in emerging economies and weak domestic demand also leave limited scope to redirect goods shut out of Europe to other markets.
China’s Opposition to an “EU Version of Section 301”
According to China’s Ministry of Commerce on October 2, a ministry spokesperson said in a written question-and-answer exchange with reporters the previous day: “If the EU insists on implementing discriminatory restrictions against Chinese companies and products, China will respond resolutely to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industry.” What provoked Beijing was a trade defense policy toward China reportedly being developed by the French and German governments. The two countries are said to be drafting a joint document urging the European Commission to swiftly establish a mechanism equivalent to a “European version of Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act,” granting the EU new powers to deny Chinese products market access. Just as the United States has used Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose steep tariffs, the proposal would give the Commission legal authority to bar products from specified third countries from the European single market altogether.
A senior official familiar with the document said the mechanism, if introduced, would give the EU sweeping enforcement powers to shut certain Chinese products out of its internal market entirely within 24 hours when necessary. Spanish outlet Dossier Bruselas also reported that the two governments were finalizing a reform proposal to substantially ease the conditions for activating the EU’s existing Anti-Coercion Instrument (ACI), allowing the Commission to swiftly impose retaliatory tariffs and import and export restrictions on its own authority without a unanimous vote by member states.
China’s Ministry of Commerce immediately condemned the proposals. The spokesperson described them as “typical protectionist and unilateral measures” that would “disrupt bilateral trade and the stability of global supply chains.” The spokesperson continued: “The EU has itself been a victim of such instruments and should not impose on others what it would not accept for itself,” adding that “if the EU, which has always portrayed itself as a defender of multilateralism, takes the lead in violating World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, it will deal a severe blow to the rules-based multilateral trading system.” The spokesperson said: “If the EU increases pressure on China while simultaneously engaging in dialogue and negotiations, it will seriously undermine mutual trust, obstruct overall progress in negotiations and affect the broader framework of bilateral economic and trade cooperation.” The spokesperson added: “We urge the EU to remain on the right track of managing differences through dialogue. We will closely monitor its subsequent actions.”
Record Trade Deficit and Manufacturing Weakness Behind EU Import Restrictions
A substantial trade deficit underlies the EU’s drive to tighten trade restrictions. The bloc’s trade deficit with China reached a record approximately $406.7 billion last year, up 15% from the previous year. That amounts to a deficit accumulating at roughly $1.13 billion a day. The EU is therefore pursuing direct limits on import volumes in its negotiations with China. According to Euronews, the European Commission has proposed import quotas on certain Chinese products. When the two sides launched negotiations in June to address trade imbalances, they set this month as the deadline for tangible results. The Commission reportedly delayed protective measures for the bloc’s chemicals industry, which faces competition from Chinese products, to preserve room for negotiation. China has, however, rejected voluntary restrictions on its electric vehicle exports, leaving disagreements over product-specific volume adjustments unresolved.
Declining production and exports across major manufacturing industries have also lent urgency to Europe’s response. Steel is a prominent example. Excess supply from China, high energy costs and U.S. tariffs have combined to depress both exports and production among European steelmakers. According to the European Steel Association, EU steel exports to the United States fell 29% year on year in the first half of this year. The United States’ 50% tariff on imported steel contributed to a 20% decline in EU steelmakers’ overall exports during the same period. Exports to Türkiye, India and China each fell by at least 18%. Crude steel production within the bloc declined 3% last year to 126 million metric tons and fell a further 1% in January–May this year.

Closer Coordination on China in Steel and Electric Vehicles
With steel production and exports remaining weak, the EU agreed to work with major importing countries to address excess supply from China. The “Milwaukee Framework,” setting out a coordinated response, was adopted at a ministerial meeting of the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity in Milwaukee, United States, on September 30. The framework includes collecting and disclosing information on the country where steel was initially melted and poured, and sharing data among members to identify suspicious trade flows. The aim is to trace the production routes of steel subsequently processed in third countries and determine whether tariffs have been circumvented. Reducing market-distorting subsidies and government support that encourages capacity expansion was also identified as a joint priority. At the meeting, U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer said countries would adopt measures suited to their own circumstances while coordinating their responses.
The EU has also moved to strengthen coordination with neighboring trading partners on China in the automotive sector. According to electric vehicle publication CnEVPost, the EU called on the United Kingdom to raise tariffs on Chinese EVs and closely align its trade policy toward China with the bloc’s. Britain did not join the EU when it introduced additional tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024. Concerns have emerged within the bloc that these tariff differences could allow Chinese products to enter its market through the United Kingdom. The Commission therefore decided to link British companies’ inclusion in “Made in Europe” policies, which concentrate subsidies and public procurement benefits on manufacturers within the bloc, to trade policy coordination. With Britain seeking eligibility for its automotive, chemicals and energy supply chains, the EU is effectively making access to benefits in its market a negotiating condition.
European Restrictions, Emerging-Market Barriers and Weak Domestic Demand: China’s Triple Export Challenge
As Europe draws neighboring trading partners into coordinated trade measures against China, Beijing faces the prospect of shrinking export markets. China has offset export losses in the United States through increased sales elsewhere, making additional European restrictions a potentially significant constraint on its export strategy. According to the European Central Bank (ECB), Chinese exports to the United States fell 20% last year, a decline of $104 billion from the previous year. Over the same period, exports to the euro area rose 8%, while shipments to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) increased 13%. Exports to Africa and Latin America also expanded, allowing China’s total exports to maintain growth of 5.5%. Demand across these regions compensated for declining shipments to the United States, but additional European restrictions could narrow one of the principal outlets China has secured.
Redirecting goods excluded from Europe to emerging economies also faces constraints. articles.title: Poland seeks stronger economic ties with India as EU trade deal advances - Times of Oman
articles.summary: Poland seeks stronger economic ties with India as EU trade deal advances  Times of Oman
articles.full_text:
Poland is seeking to strengthen its economic and strategic partnership with India following the conclusion of the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA), with Warsaw viewing the deal as an opportunity to expand trade, investment and cooperation across Central and Eastern Europe (CEE).
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk visited New Delhi on October 21, 2026, leading a delegation of nearly 100 companies. The visit was the first by a Polish prime minister to India since 2010 and followed the conclusion of negotiations on the EU-India trade agreement on January 27, 2026.
Negotiations for the agreement began in 2007 but stalled in 2013 before resuming in 2022. The deal connects two economic blocs accounting for approximately a quarter of global gross domestic product (GDP).
The European Commission expects EU exports of goods to India to double by 2032, with tariffs eliminated or reduced on 96.6 per cent of goods. The agreement also envisages improved access to India's services market and a quota-based system for automotive trade.
The agreement is expected to be signed in Brussels in December, with implementation targeted for early 2027, subject to the necessary approval, including consent from the European Parliament.
The agreement comes amid growing efforts by India and Europe to diversify supply chains and reduce strategic dependencies, particularly in response to tariff policies in the United States and export controls in China.
Polish-Indian trade stood at approximately $5.7 billion in 2024, making Poland India's largest trade and investment partner in Central and Eastern Europe. However, bilateral trade remains considerably smaller than India's trade with Germany and France.
Analysts note that tariff reductions alone will not guarantee an immediate increase in business. Their benefits will depend on companies establishing commercial relationships and developing investment partnerships.
Potential areas of cooperation include defence technology, military drones, electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, quantum technologies, critical minerals and space. Polish electric bus manufacturer Solaris, through its joint venture with India's JBM Auto, offers an example of industrial cooperation.
During Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Warsaw in August 2024, the two countries established a strategic partnership and set a target of doubling bilateral trade by 2030.
Tusk has also promoted Poland as a gateway for Indian businesses seeking access to the wider European market. However, experts argue that Central and Eastern European countries could secure greater benefits by coordinating their engagement with India rather than competing individually.
The visit highlighted the potential for cooperation through the Visegrád group, comprising Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic. Discussions involving Indian and Visegrád foreign ministers could provide a framework for deeper regional engagement.
India's support for Poland's aspirations for a permanent place in the G20 was another significant aspect of the discussions, although the joint statement stopped short of guaranteeing membership. Poland, meanwhile, reiterated its support for India's bid for a permanent seat on an expanded United Nations Security Council.
Despite expanding economic ties, India's relationship with Russia remains a concern for Poland and other CEE countries, particularly in the context of the war in Ukraine.
The joint statement focused largely on the conflict's implications for food and energy security, while both sides emphasised the importance of a comprehensive and lasting peace consistent with the UN Charter.
The EU-India agreement is unlikely to transform Central and Eastern European economies immediately. Its long-term impact will depend on translating diplomatic engagement into commercial contracts, strengthening regional coordination and managing differences over Russia.
The agreement's anticipated signing and subsequent implementation in 2027 will provide an early indication of whether the region can turn the emerging partnership into tangible economic and strategic gains.

Maharashtra has proposed setting up a chemical industry park near Vadhvan Port in Dahanu taluka, Palghar district, with land allocation of between 2,500 and 5,000 acres. The state government is seeking central approval under the Grand Chemical Park scheme to attract investment, strengthen industrial infrastructure and expand chemical manufacturing.
Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis announced the proposal during the inauguration of India Chem 2026. He also said the state was preparing a dedicated chemical industry policy, which is expected to be announced in the first week of November. The policy is intended to encourage investment, simplify regulatory procedures and support expansion in the chemical sector.
The proposed site’s proximity to Vadhvan Port could support the development of industrial infrastructure and manufacturing clusters, while offering logistical advantages to chemical companies and related industries. The scheme requires a minimum land area of 2,000 acres, making the proposed allocation eligible in principle, subject to formal approval and compliance with other conditions.

The initiative is intended to promote technological capabilities and innovation across strategic industries. India will have a “strong comparative advantage” in the trade deal being negotiated with the United States, Union commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said on Thursday, adding that no farmers' interests would be compromised in the agreement.
Goyal said that the people of India would “celebrate” once details of the deal are released. The Union commerce minister stressed that India was “focused on protecting” sensitive sectors and getting a comparative advantage in trade agreements in order to export more.
A country's comparative advantage refers to its ability to produce a good or service at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.

On the contrary, India will stand at a very strong comparative advantage.”
The Union commerce and industry minister said that India, through its trade deals, was not just looking at market access. He said investments and services were also an important part of negotiations.
‘US FTA politicised by few elements’
Goyal also made a veiled reference to the Opposition's criticism of the trade agreement under negotiation with the US, saying the deal was “sometimes politicised by a few elements.”
“The US free trade agreement is sometimes sought to be politicised by a few elements. I don't even know whether they deserve any comment because that's probably lack of knowledge, Details are not yet fully out. I don't know what they are criticising,” Goyal said.
The Union minister said he had yet to come across “a single criticism” or flaw in the eight FTAs already negotiated by the Centre. “I dare say, none of the FTAS finalised by the Modi government had found a single criticism or any flaw. I have yet to come across anybody who could find a singe flaw in any of the 8 FTA concluded,” Goyal added.
India has so far announced FTAs with the European Union, United Kingdom, New Zealand, Oman, Australia, United Arab Emirates and Mauritius. This trade agreement is between India and four members states of the European Free Trade Association – Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland.

The India-US trade agreement is in its “last mile”, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said last week while speaking about efforts by the two countries to find common ground on the deal they have negotiated for more than a year. However, Jaishankar added that “it’s never done till it’s done”, while adding that the “last mile” often poses challenges.
He said the negotiating teams were working through these, while refusing to elaborate further.
US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who came to India this month for a three-day official visit, have also spoken about the progress in negotiations. When Rubio was on his India visit, Trump said the agreement was “pretty close”, while adding that it “could be a much different kind of deal.” Following his meeting with Jaishankar in Mumbai during his visit, Rubio too made similar remarks.

articles.title: India-Brazil bilateral trade set to reach USD 20 billion; focus on critical minerals, AI, defence: Envoy - India's News.Net
articles.summary: India-Brazil bilateral trade set to reach USD 20 billion; focus on critical minerals, AI, defence: Envoy  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
By Sahil Pandey
New Delhi [India], October 31 (ANI): Brazil's Ambassador to India, Kenneth Felix Haczynski da Nobrega, on Friday highlighted the growing strategic and economic partnership between the two countries, saying bilateral trade is expected to soon reach USD 20 billion, with cooperation expanding across critical minerals, defence, energy, pharmaceuticals and artificial intelligence.
Addressing an event to celebrate Brazil's National Day, the envoy said the two countries were entering a new phase of bilateral engagement ahead of the upcoming 80th anniversary of diplomatic relations, with political commitment and growing business ties providing fresh momentum to the partnership.
"Political vision and business dynamism are converging to take Brazil-India relations to a new level," he said, underlining the growing economic engagement between the two countries.
Highlighting India's emergence as Brazil's fifth-largest trading partner, the ambassador said concrete progress had also been made in negotiations to expand the trade agreement between India and the Southern Common Market (MERCOSUR).
He noted that major Brazilian companies were expanding their presence in India, with aerospace major Embraer emerging as a prominent new entrant. India's foreign direct investment stock in Brazil has also increased significantly, with investments from leading Indian companies reaching USD 10 billion, he said.
The ambassador attributed the growing economic engagement to more than 150 business and technology missions exchanged between the two countries over the past three years.
On cooperation in emerging technologies and strategic sectors, da Nobrega said India and Brazil were strengthening partnerships in energy, defence, agriculture, healthcare, digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence.
"Just recently, we agreed to connect our efforts on rare earths and critical minerals. We also built new partnerships in pharmaceutical research and innovation, and launched a broad digital partnership," he said.
Describing mutual trust as a key strength of bilateral relations, he said the partnership had developed over eight decades and was now delivering tangible results in areas critical to the future competitiveness and resilience of both economies.
"In those uncertain years and in this uncertain world we are living in, trust is not just an asset; it is a strategic advantage," he said.
Reflecting on bilateral cooperation in multilateral forums, the Brazilian envoy praised India's leadership during its BRICS chairmanship, particularly its ability to bring member countries together for discussions on challenging global issues.
He said Brazil and India had worked in "full synergy" within BRICS under India's stewardship, highlighting India's convening power and diplomatic deftness in ensuring that all members remained engaged in dialogue.
The two countries had also strengthened their environmental cooperation following COP30, with Brazil assuming co-chairmanship alongside India of the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) and the Global Biofuels Alliance, he said.
The ambassador also recalled the state visits of Prime Minister Narendra Modi to Brazil in 2025 and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to India earlier this year, saying the visits provided strong political backing to expanding cooperation in economic and technological fields.
Looking ahead, he said the two countries would also seek to deepen cultural engagement, with Brazil planning to extend to India in 2027 celebrations marking the 100th birth anniversary of legendary Brazilian musician Antonio Carlos Jobim, popularly known as Tom Jobim.
Jobim was one of the leading figures behind Bossa Nova, the Brazilian musical genre that gained international recognition by blending European musical influences, jazz and African rhythms.
The ambassador also referred to Brazil's recent peaceful electoral exercise, saying more than 150 million Brazilians had participated in the polls, with voter turnout reaching its highest level in over two decades.
He described the election as a reflection of Brazil's democratic traditions and civic identity.
India and Brazil are key partners in the Global South and work closely across multilateral platforms, including BRICS, G20 and the United Nations. Both countries have been seeking to expand cooperation in trade, technology, energy transition and reform of global governance institutions. (ANI)

NEW DELHI: A preliminary framework for negotiations between the United States and Iran proposes transferring Tehran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country or reducing its enrichment levels, alongside reopening the Strait of Hormuz to international shipping within seven days of an initial understanding, Al Arabiya English reported on Saturday.
The draft framework, which was obtained exclusively by the news platform, also identifies China as a potential guarantor to ensure the implementation and sustainability of any agreement. It proposes holding direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran in Doha instead of Istanbul.
Under the proposed arrangement, Iran would undertake commitments on its nuclear programme and maritime security in exchange for US steps to ease sanctions, blockades and other economic restrictions.
The framework also envisages an independent verification mechanism to assess compliance before each phase of implementation. This would ensure that neither side makes substantial concessions without corresponding and independently verifiable commitments from the other.
A separate dispute-resolution mechanism involving mediators and guarantor countries has also been proposed to address delays or violations and prevent a fresh escalation of military tensions, according to Al Arabiya English.
Qatar steps up diplomatic outreach
Diplomatic efforts to revive a ceasefire between Washington and Tehran gathered pace on Friday, with a Qatari delegation arriving in the Iranian capital for consultations, Iranian state news agency IRNA reported.
The delegation, led by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister, arrived on Friday morning and was coordinating its efforts with the United States.
Meanwhile, a letter from US Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei was reportedly delivered by Qatari envoys. The communication was welcomed in Tehran for proposing a fresh diplomatic pathway to prevent further American military strikes, according to reports.
Trump says US in no hurry to end war
The diplomatic developments come amid US President Donald Trump's assertion that Washington is in no hurry to end its conflict with Iran, describing the hostilities as "not a typical war".
Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump claimed that Tehran remained interested in negotiations but was facing domestic financial difficulties, including an inability to pay military personnel and law enforcement officers.
“There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking,” Trump told reporters.
“But look, they're not paying their soldiers, they're not paying their police. They're in a lot of trouble. And we have time, frankly. It's a war, but it's not a typical war; we've been there for seven months,” he added.
Trump also played down the financial burden of the military campaign, claiming that Washington's expenditure on the conflict was relatively low and had been offset by gains elsewhere.
“We're spending very little money, relatively speaking. I heard somebody say, you're spending money. I said, well, any money we spent, we've more than made up for in a place called Venezuela, like by 10 times...” he said.
However, he did not provide figures to substantiate his claim about recovering the cost of the military campaign through Venezuela.
Despite expressing confidence that the US had time on its side, Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of renewed military action against Iran. He previously referred to the prospect of launching “another little Epic Fury”, a reference to the initial US military operation against Tehran, while also suggesting that a “big and good” agreement could still be reached.
Turkey also engages Washington
Parallel diplomatic efforts continued as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of a G20 ministerial gathering in the United States on Friday.
According to Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency, the discussions covered the ongoing negotiations between Washington and Tehran, regional developments and bilateral relations.
The meeting followed a telephone conversation between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Trump earlier in the week. During the call, Ankara conveyed its concerns over maritime routes and expressed support for diplomatic initiatives to reduce regional tensions.
The proposed framework comes amid continuing differences between Washington and Tehran over Iran's nuclear programme, sanctions and the US blockade of Iranian ports. Whether the latest diplomatic efforts can translate into a lasting agreement remains uncertain.

The three-year deferral of Bangladesh’s graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category gives the country time to address energy, logistics and financing constraints and to negotiate trade deals before it loses duty-free access, say exporters and economists. They stress that the time will count only if reforms begin now.
The United Nations General Assembly in early hours on Friday (Bangladesh time) moved the graduation date from 24 November 2026 to 24 November 2029. Nepal received the same extension.
Prime Minister's Adviser Mahdi Amin said the extra time would allow the government to prepare the economy, industries, export-import sector, businesses and employment for the transition.
"The significance of this decision lies in continuing inclusive development, so that LDC graduation cannot create unexpected pressure on the country's economy and peoples' livelihoods," he said.
In a social media post, he said the outcome reflected Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's "effective leadership" in building global support for policies to protect Bangladesh's interests.
What is at stake
According to government estimates, Bangladeshi exporters have duty-free access to 38 countries and trade blocs under LDC-specific arrangements, and about 73% of total exports benefit from such preferences.
The government estimates that graduation could expose exports to an average tariff of around 12.5%, though the impact would vary by product and destination.
Bangladesh exported goods worth $48 billion in FY26, of which readymade garments (RMG) accounted for about 81%.
Time to modernise industry
Shovon Islam, managing director and owner of Sparrow Group and a former director of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), told Daily Sun the extension offered "valuable breathing space to protect employment, strengthen competitiveness and prepare for a sustainable transition".
He said manufacturers could use the period to modernise factories, raise productivity and diversify into man-made fibres and higher-value apparel. The extension would also give investors and international buyers greater certainty for sourcing decisions, he added.
BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said the industry had long sought more preparation time. He said the country must use it to improve infrastructure and logistics.
Mohiuddin Rubel, another former BGMEA director, called for stronger backward linkages, better infrastructure and a more varied export basket. He described the extension as a "lifeline" and said Bangladesh might not get another such opportunity.
Room to negotiate market access
Several of those interviewed said the period should be used to secure market access through negotiations.
Mahmud Hasan Khan said the country should pursue free trade agreements (FTAs) with major trading partners where necessary. Rubel said competitor countries were already seeking bilateral arrangements to protect their market access, and Bangladesh should do the same.
Fahmida Khatun, distinguished fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said Bangladesh should engage early with major export destinations to prepare for possible changes in tariffs and trade preferences after graduation.
Rubel noted that graduation would not automatically end all duty-free access, as trading partners have different preferential arrangements.
Mustafa Abid Khan, chief executive of the Bangladesh Foreign Trade Institute (BFTI), said the additional time would help the country prepare for changes in trade rules, particularly on intellectual property. Certain LDC-specific flexibilities under World Trade Organization rules will lapse after graduation, requiring stronger intellectual property protection and enforcement capacity, he said. Trade negotiations would be central to retaining preferential access to major destinations, he added.
Diversification and the EU framework
Fahmida said the extension would not by itself resolve structural weaknesses. "Effective reforms are needed in trade, revenue collection, banking and infrastructure," she said. She urged greater investment in pharmaceuticals, agro-processing, leather, light engineering, jute products and information technology to reduce dependence on garments.
The European Union, Bangladesh's largest export destination, offers a three-year transition under its Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) after LDC graduation. Bangladesh will also need to meet the conditions for retaining preferential access, including possible qualification for GSP+.
The new EU GSP framework, due to apply from January 2027, places greater emphasis on implementing international conventions on labour rights, human rights, environmental protection and governance. Improvements in labour standards, environmental compliance and institutional governance will therefore bear directly on Bangladesh's position in the European market.
Warnings against delay
Exporters cautioned that the deferral does not remove existing constraints.
"The deadline has changed, but our weaknesses remain: unreliable energy, high financing costs, slow logistics and insufficient productivity," Shovon said.
He noted that buyers' expectations on labour rights, sustainability and supply-chain traceability would keep rising, and that competitor countries would keep strengthening their positions.
"Our biggest risk is complacency," he said.
He urged that the extension be treated as a firm reform deadline, with priority for reliable energy, competitive raw-material sourcing, faster customs clearance and port operations, technological upgrading and workers' skills.
Rubel said the focus should be on action. "Rather than becoming overly excited about the postponement, we must immediately start working on the necessary reforms and preparations," he said.
Background
Bangladesh first met all three LDC graduation criteria in March 2018 and retained its eligibility in the 2021 triennial review. In the 2024 review, its gross national income per capita was $2,684, against a threshold of $1,306. Its Human Assets Index score was 77.5 against a required 66, and its Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index score was 21.9 against a ceiling of 32.
Bangladesh applied to the UN Committee for Development Policy on 18 February 2026 under its crisis-response mechanism. The committee recommended favourable consideration, and the Economic and Social Council recommended on 21 July that the General Assembly decide the matter. The country had earlier received a two-year extension of its preparatory period because of the COVID-19 pandemic.

                India’s Infrastructure Transformation: From Connectivity to Capacity
                प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                12 AUG 2026 19:12 PM
            
                
 Building the Foundation of Growth
India’s infrastructure landscape has undergone a major transformation over the past 12 years. From transport and logistics to housing and water, infrastructure development has moved towards integrated planning and large-scale expansion. This has strengthened connectivity, improved access to essential services and created the foundations for sustained economic growth. Public capital expenditure has risen from about ₹2 lakh crore in FY 2014–15 to ₹12.2 lakh crore in FY 2026–27, supporting this advancement.                                                                                                                                                    
 A New Era of Rail Mobility 
Indian Railways is moving towards faster, safer and more modern mobility. Electrification, advanced safety systems, high-speed rail and new-generation trains are reshaping the rail network.
	- Railway budget increased from ₹32,000 crore in 2014–15 to ₹2.78 lakh crore in FY2026–27. 
- Rail electrification increased from about 20% before 2014 to 99.6% by July 2026. 
- 162 Vande Bharat, 2 Vande Bharat Sleeper Services and 72 Amrit Bharat services have improved connectivity and travel experience. 
- The Kavach Version 4.0 has been commissioned on 2,633 route km as of July 2026.
- The Mumbai–Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail Corridor is being developed over a 508 km route with a design speed of 350 kmph.
- Of the 1,340 stations identified under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme, redevelopment has been completed for 261 stations as on 18 July 2026.
- First indigenously developed Hydrogen Fuel Cell Trainset has been launched in July 2026. It is a 10-coach train with capacity for around 2,600 passengers, running on the Jind–Sonipat section. It generates its own electricity onboard with water vapour and heat as the only by-product.
 
 
 
 Roads and Highways Connecting India
A wider and more capable road network is bringing regions closer. The expansion of National Highways, rural roads and major corridors is enabling smoother movement of people and goods.
	- India has the world’s second-largest road network at 63.73 lakh km. 
- Length of national highways increased by about 61%, from 91,287 km in FY 14 to 1,46,572 km in March 2026. 
- The length of four-lane and above national highways increased from 18,371 km in 2014 to 45,516 km. 
- The length of roads increased from 3.86 lakh km during 2000–2014 to 4.11 lakh km during 2014–2026 under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana. Since September 2024, PMGSY-IV has been launched with an objective to provide connectivity to 25,000 unconnected habitations by the year 2029.
- Under Bharatmala, 22,590 km of roads have been completed till 31 March 2026.
 Bridges and Tunnels: Engineering New Frontiers
Engineering breakthroughs are overcoming some of India’s most demanding geographical challenges. These projects are opening new routes across difficult terrain.
	- Chenab Bridge (2025): World's highest railway arch bridge, standing 359 m above the Chenab River; 1,315 m steel structure strengthening Jammu–Srinagar connectivity. 
- Anji Khad Bridge (2025): India's first cable-stayed railway bridge, in Jammu & Kashmir. 
- Pamban Bridge (2025): India's first vertical-lift railway sea bridge, connecting Rameswaram to the mainland; 2.07 km with a 72.5 m vertical lift span. 
- Z-Morh/Sonamarg Tunnel (2025): 12 km tunnel providing all-weather access through avalanche-prone terrain in J&K, improving movement towards Ladakh. 
- Sudarshan Setu (2024): 2.32 km bridge connecting Okha with Beyt Dwarka, Gujarat. 
- Atal Tunnel (2020): 9.02 km — world's longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet, connecting Manali and Lahaul-Spiti.
- Dr. Syama Prasad Mukherjee Tunnel (2017): 9 km all-weather tunnel between Jammu and Srinagar, cutting travel time by ~2 hours. 
 Civil Aviation and Regional Air Access
Air connectivity is reaching more cities, towns and remote regions. The expansion of airports, UDAN routes and digital passenger services is making flying more accessible across the country.
	- UDAN connected 95 airports, heliports, and water aerodromes through 679 routes, benefiting over 1.68 crore passengers as on 15 July 2026. 
- Operational airports increased from 74 in 2014 to 165 in July 2026.
- 25 greenfield airports have been approved after 2014.  
- Digi Yatra is active at 38 airports. The app has enabled over 10 crore seamless journeys with over 2.4 crore downloads.  
- Modified UDAN has been approved in March 2026 for FY 2026–27 to FY 2035–36 with an outlay of ₹28,840 crore, envisioning 100 new airports and 200 modern helipads to strengthen last-mile regional air connectivity.
 Metro: The Rise of Mass Urban Transit
India’s urban mobility network is expanding in scale and scope. Metro connectivity now spans more cities, while innovative systems are opening new possibilities for urban transport.
	- Metro network expanded from 248 km in 2014 to over 1,155 km in 2026.  
- Cities with metro connectivity increased from 5 to 26, while daily ridership crossed 1.15 crore passengers. 
- Kolkata operationalised India’s first underwater metro tunnel in 2024. 
- Kochi operationalised India’s first Water Metro system with the first boat launched in December 2021.
 India’s Maritime Momentum
India is strengthening its maritime backbone to support a growing economy and expanding trade. Investments in ports, waterways and maritime infrastructure are creating a more capable and connected ecosystem.
	- Major ports’ cargo handling capacity nearly doubled from 873 MMTPA in 2014 to 1,728 MMTPA in 2026. 
- Vessel turnaround time improved from 94 hours to 48.8 hours in 2025-26. 
- Major ports collectively handled 915.17 MT of cargo during FY 2025-26, increasing from 581 MT in FY 2014-15.
- The Sagarmala Programme strengthened port-led development, coastal connectivity, and logistics integration.
- National waterways increased from 5 in 2014 to 111 in 2026, of which 32 are operational. 
- India became the world's No. 1 ship-recycling nation in 2025, with its global share rising from 30.1% (2024) to 35.4% (2025) — recycling 2.99 million gross tons (GT), up nearly 60% from 1.86 million GT in 2024.
- Jawaharlal Nehru Port ranked 22nd as per the Container Port Performance Index (CPPI) 2025, published by the World Bank.
-  Bharat Maritime Insurance Pool (BMIP) has been launched on 12 May 2026. It is a USD 1.5 billion domestic insurance pool with a sovereign guarantee of USD 1.4 billion (₹12,980 crore), covering Hull & Machinery, Cargo, Protection and Indemnity, and War risk for Indian-flagged/controlled vessels. As on 29th July 2026, a total of 1608 policies covering Cargo War risks and Hull War risks have been issued under the Pool.
 Strengthening Logistics and Industrial Capacity
Infrastructure is increasingly being planned as an interconnected network supporting industry and trade. From GatiShakti to industrial corridors, the focus is on improving coordination, efficiency and manufacturing capacity.
	- PM GatiShakti National Master Plan integrated infrastructure planning across 58 Ministries and Departments using over 3,291 data layers. 
- As on 11 August 2026, 396 infrastructure projects with a total estimated cost of about ₹18.66 Lakh Crore have been evaluated through the Network Planning Group mechanism. Out of these, 256 projects have been sanctioned and 198 projects are under implementation. 
- The National Logistics Policy has strengthened multimodal logistics efficiency and supply chain integration.
- PRAGATI reviewed 382 projects worth over ₹85 lakh crore and resolved 2,958 issues.
- Over 4,220 industrial parks are mapped on the India Industrial Land Bank (IILB).
	- 272 plug-and-play industrial parks are operational across the country.
- 20 industrial smart cities have been approved across 7 industrial corridors.
- The BHAVYA scheme has been approved in March 2026 to develop 100 new plug-and-play industrial parks. 
- BHAVYA Rasayan Scheme has been approved on 24 July 2026, with an outlay of ₹3,030 crore. The scheme will be implemented over five years, from FY2026–27 to FY2030–31. 
- 7 Pradhan Mantri MITRA Parks have been proposed to strengthen the manufacturing ecosystem.
 Water, Housing and Urban Development
The infrastructure push extends directly to people’s homes and everyday needs. From tap-water access and affordable housing to urban renewal, these efforts are shaping better living conditions across rural and urban India.
	- Under Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM), rural tap water coverage increased from 3.23 crore in 2019 to around 15.91 crore households as on 10th August 2026.
- JJM 2.0 has been approved in March 2026. The mission has been extended to December 2028, with an enhanced outlay of ₹8.69 lakh crore. 
	- Under Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Urban (PMAY-U), 99.25 lakh houses have been completed as on 12 August 2026. Around 96% of houses under PMAY-U 2.0 are allotted to women.
- Under Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Grameen (PMAY-G), out of the 3.91 crore houses sanctioned, 3.13 crore houses have been completed as on 12 August 2026.  Nearly 75% of the houses sanctioned under PMAY-G are either in the name of women or under joint ownership.
- The SWAMIH Fund launched in 2019 delivered over 63,000 homes, benefiting around 2.52 lakh people as of June 2026.
- Under AMRUT and AMRUT 2.0, projects worth about ₹2.79 lakh crore have been sanctioned since 2015. 
- Under Smart Cities Mission, a total of 7,790 projects worth ₹1,56,257 crore have been completed as of March 2026.

articles.summary: The Economic Cost Of India’s Trade Suspension – OpEd  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- The suspension of India–Pakistan trade after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack, including India’s closure of the Attari Integrated Check Post, has further constrained an already limited commercial relationship and disrupted livelihoods tied to the Attari–Wagah crossing.
- Small traders, freight handlers, transport operators and warehouse workers face the sharpest immediate losses, while repeated political interruptions undermine the economic value of India’s land-port infrastructure and broader regional connectivity ambitions.
- The article argues that security concerns and economic cooperation need not be mutually exclusive and that prolonged border closures impose lasting social and opportunity costs on communities when carefully negotiated alternatives remain possible.
Political tensions between India and Pakistan have repeatedly demonstrated how quickly security crises can dismantle economic opportunities painstakingly built over time. The suspension of bilateral trade following the Pahalgam attack in April 2025 offers another example of the economic consequences of allowing political confrontation to overshadow regional connectivity. While governments have legitimate security concerns to address, the closure of commercial routes also affects traders, transport workers, logistics companies and communities whose livelihoods depend on cross-border economic activity. The consequences extend beyond diplomatic relations, raising questions about employment, regional development and the long-term prospects for economic cooperation in South Asia.
The Attari–Wagah crossing has historically served as a significant gateway for trade and people-to-people contact between India and Pakistan. Alongside other historical transport links, it represented the possibility that geography could facilitate economic cooperation rather than remain a source of strategic competition. The suspension of trade following the Pahalgam attack in April 2025 dealt another blow to an already restricted trading relationship. India announced the closure of the Attari Integrated Check Post as part of its response to the attack, while Pakistan subsequently announced the suspension of trade with India. These measures further constrained an economic relationship that had already deteriorated following earlier political and security crises.
The immediate consequences of such decisions are often felt most acutely by those with the least influence over policymaking. Small traders, freight handlers, customs-related workers, transport operators and warehouse employees depend on the regular movement of goods to sustain their incomes. When commercial traffic stops, the effects spread throughout the local economy. Businesses lose customers, logistics services face reduced demand, and workers may experience declining earnings or unemployment. Although the precise scale of employment losses associated with the latest suspension requires independently verified data, the underlying economic mechanism is clear: prolonged restrictions impose costs on communities whose livelihoods depend on cross-border commerce.
India’s broader land-port development strategy illustrates the importance New Delhi attaches to cross-border infrastructure. The Land Ports Authority of India has pursued the development of integrated facilities intended to improve border management, facilitate trade and strengthen passenger movement. However, infrastructure investment alone cannot guarantee economic returns. The effectiveness of a land port depends on predictable commercial arrangements, functioning transport links, regulatory coordination and sustained demand. When political disputes repeatedly interrupt trade, the economic value of border infrastructure is diminished.
This creates a strategic contradiction. Governments invest in modern terminals, roads and logistics facilities to facilitate the movement of goods, yet political confrontation can render these assets underutilised. The costs include not only lost commercial transactions but also the opportunity cost of infrastructure that could otherwise support employment, investment and regional development. For India and Pakistan, where geographical proximity offers obvious advantages, the prolonged interruption of formal trade represents a missed opportunity to build more resilient commercial relationships.
The consequences also extend to regional connectivity. Pakistan occupies a geographically significant position between South Asia, Afghanistan, Iran and the wider Central Asian region. Under more cooperative political conditions, improved commercial links could support the movement of goods between regional markets and connect producers with new consumers. India, meanwhile, has long sought greater access to Central Asian markets and resources. Its pursuit of alternative connectivity arrangements, including the International North–South Transport Corridor, reflects the importance it attaches to diversifying trade routes.
Land access through Pakistan could, under appropriate political and commercial conditions, offer India another route towards Afghanistan and Central Asia. Yet such a possibility remains constrained by the unresolved political relationship, security concerns and competing regional interests. Alternative corridors can reduce dependence on individual routes, but they also involve infrastructure costs, transit arrangements and geopolitical considerations. The economic viability of any route must therefore be assessed through comparative analysis rather than assumptions that one corridor is universally cheaper or more efficient.
The wider social implications deserve equal attention. Employment generated by border commerce can support household incomes, small enterprises and local investment. Its decline may intensify financial pressures, particularly where alternative employment is limited. Governments should therefore consider the economic needs of affected communities when introducing prolonged restrictions and develop support mechanisms for workers and businesses exposed to sudden policy changes.
For Pakistan and India, the broader lesson is that security and economic cooperation need not be treated as mutually exclusive objectives. Sustainable trade requires political trust, credible safeguards and a willingness to address disputes through established channels. Even when comprehensive normalisation remains politically difficult, practical arrangements that reduce risks to legitimate commerce could help protect livelihoods and preserve the possibility of future cooperation.
Ultimately, the closure of a border is never merely a diplomatic gesture. It affects workers, businesses, communities and the infrastructure connecting neighbouring economies. The suspension of India–Pakistan trade demonstrates how quickly political confrontation can undermine commercial opportunities and regional connectivity. If South Asia is to realise its economic potential, its governments must recognise that security decisions carry wider social and economic consequences. Borders may be necessary for regulating sovereignty and managing risks, but they should not become permanent barriers to prosperity when carefully negotiated alternatives remain possible.

articles.full_text:
New Delhi says sensitive agricultural interests will remain protected as Washington seeks greater access to the country's farm market
India will not compromise the interests of its farmers in the trade deal it is negotiating with the US, the federal trade minister has said, amid warnings and protest calls from powerful farm groups against cheaper American agricultural imports.
New Delhi and Washington announced a framework for an interim trade agreement in February, but the pact is yet to be signed. Negotiations have faced repeated delays over market access and tariffs, and unpredictability in US tariff policies.
"Not a single sensitive interest of our farmers or any stakeholder has been compromised," Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said at an industrial development conference in New Delhi on Thursday. He maintained that India would gain a strong competitive advantage once the agreement's details are made public.
Sensitive sectors including dairy, meat, poultry, maize, cereals, and genetically modified foods would remain protected, a February background paper published by India's Commerce Ministry said. The concessions include limited, reduced-duty import quotas for almonds, walnuts, and pistachios, while tariff reductions on certain other products would be phased in over up to ten years.
There would be zero additional US duties on selected Indian agricultural exports worth $1.36 billion, including tea, coffee, spices, and processed foods, according to the government.
The Samyukt Kisan Morcha, a coalition of more than 100 farmer organizations, has called for protests on November 26 and warned that subsidized American imports could depress domestic prices and hurt rural incomes. It has also demanded disclosure of the agreement's terms.
The All-India Kisan Sabha, another farmer organization, separately warned against opening up India's dairy market, arguing that cheaper US products could put pressure on milk procurement prices and rural households dependent on dairy farming.
Both Goyal and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio have said recently that the deal is near the finish line. However, some media reports have said talks have stalled as New Delhi refuses to accept a proposed 18% tariff rate along with concessions on farm products, and the final deal could come only after the November 3 US midterm elections.
